article_text:
国立科学博物館（東京・上野公園）で10月31日から2027年2月21日まで開催される特別展「生きものたちの性」。アンバサダーで、音声ガイドナビゲーターを務めるラランドのサーヤさんとニシダさんが音声ガイド収録を終え、コメントを発表しました。

収録で二人は普段のバラエティで見せる姿とは異なる“真面目な一面”を意識したといいます。

ニシダさんは「僕らのファンだけじゃなくて、本当に動物や植物に興味があって来る人もいるので、『なんだこの人たちは』と思われないようにしたかった。真面目に向き合う部分を多めにしました。誰よりも性に向き合ったと思います」と笑いを交えながらも収録への本気度をのぞかせました。

サーヤさんは「原稿が本当に面白くて、『へぇ』『なるほど』の連続でした。思わず『え、マジか!?』と言いそうになるくらい興味深い内容でした。生きものたちの性の多様さや奥深さをぜひ会場で体感してほしいです」と来場を呼びかけました。

ラランドがナビゲーターを務める音声ガイドは、会場レンタル版が650円、アプリ配信版が800円です。

◇前売りチケット 美術展ナビチケットアプリで発売中！

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班）

特別展「生きものたちの性」

会期：2026年10月31日(土)～2027年2月21日(日)

開館時間：9時～17時(入場は16時30分まで)

今週末に見たいアートイベントTOP5：真鍋大度らが挑む木工とAIの融合、東京の16作家が示す新たな視点

関東地方の美術館・ギャラリーを中心に、現在開催されている展覧会の中でも特におすすめの展示をピックアップ！ アートな週末を楽しもう！

1. T3 PHOTO FESTIVAL TOKYO 2026（八重洲・日本橋・京橋・銀座エリアほか）

「と」を起点に、写真で巡る東京

八重洲・日本橋・京橋・銀座エリアを舞台に展開する 写真 フェスティバル「T3 PHOTO FESTIVAL TOKYO」。2026年は「と」をテーマに掲げ、「自分と他者」「自然と都市」など、異なるもののあいだにある関係性に目を向ける。二つのものを分けるだけでなく、それらを繋ぐ言葉でもある「と」に着目し、写真における撮る側と写る側、作品と見る側といった関係にも視点を広げる。

TOFROM YAESU TOWERではメイン展示ザネレ・ムホリ「ものが王冠になるとき」のほか、写真フェア「T3 PHOTO ASIA」（10月17～19日）やブックフェア「T3 BOOK MARCHE」（17・18日）、国内外のキュレーターらが写真とアジアの現在について語る「T3 Talk Program」などを実施。TODA BUILDINGではアントニー・ケアンズ＆ピータン「STUDIO＋ 拡張する現代写真 #2」、東京ミッドタウン八重洲ではルーカス・フォグリア「コンスタント・ブルーム」などが開催されている。

T3 PHOTO FESTIVAL TOKYO 2026 会期：10月3日（土）〜10月26日（月） 場所：東京八重洲・日本橋・京橋・銀座エリアほか 時間：会場により異なる 休館日：会場により異なる

2. 「座標──TOKYO ATLAS関連企画：東京都による支援作家たちの現在地」（WHAT MUSEUM）

東京で創作する作家たちの「現在地」をたどる

東京都がこれまで支援してきたアーティストやキュレーターを紹介する、国際美術展「TOKYO ATLAS」の関連展。会場の1階では、「積層する夢、浮遊する風景」をテーマに、品川周辺の歴史や埋め立て地という土地の特徴を手がかりに新たな風景を描き出す。青柳菜摘＋ 細井美裕 は、近隣の埋め立て地などをリサーチし、土木工学の知見を生かして2本の道を制作。観客が歩いて道を踏み固める行為を通じて、自分たちが今立っている場所について考えるきっかけを生み出す。このほか、陳郁文（セラ・ユウェン・チェン）、何梓羽（カ・シウ）、西村涼、佐藤浩一＋梅沢英樹、山縣瑠衣が出品する。

2階の展示は「窓から覗く幽霊、手のひらの双子座の神様」と題し、作家それぞれの身体感覚から生まれる平面作品や立体、パフォーマンスなどを通して、現代美術の現在地を提示する。大原崇嘉の《Suspensions》（2026）は、静止した石をビデオカメラで撮影し、その映像を振り子のように揺れるモニターに映し出す作品だ。動かない石と揺れる画面の関係が観客の感覚を揺さぶり、「見る」という行為に伴う身体の状態へと意識を向けさせる。ほか出品者は、ちぇんしげ、小林椋、播磨みどりら10人。

「座標──TOKYO ATLAS関連企画：東京都による支援作家たちの現在地」 会期：10月10日（土）〜12月20日（日） 場所：WHAT MUSEUM（東京都品川区東品川2-6-10 寺田倉庫G号） 時間：10:00〜17:00（入場は30分前まで） 休館日：月曜（祝日の場合は翌火曜。11月23日を除く）

3. 藤岡亜弥「Forget Me Not」（BUG）

9年前の一通のメッセージから始まった、記憶をたどる写真

写真家の藤岡亜弥（1972年生まれ）は、個人的な記憶や場所を起点に作品を制作してきた。2007年から文化庁の新進芸術家海外研修制度で約5年間ニューヨークに滞在し、2013年からは広島を拠点に活動。祖母のブラジル移民としての経験を追った「Saudade」や、ニューヨーク滞在中の5年間をもとにした「Life Studies」などを発表してきた。 木村伊兵衛写真賞 を受賞するなど、国内外で評価を得ている。

本展では、BUGのコミッションによる新シリーズ「Forget Me Not」を初公開。9年前、オーストラリア・メルボルンに住む女性から届いた一通のメッセージをきっかけに、藤岡の故郷である広島県呉市とオーストラリアを結びながら、戦後から現在にまたがってある人物をめぐる調査と撮影を続けてきた。新たな発見によって情報が重なっていく過程を、写真を通してたどっていく。

藤岡亜弥「Forget Me Not」 会期：10月14日（水）〜11月29日（日） 場所：BUG（東京都千代田区丸の内1-9-2 グラントウキョウサウスタワー1F） 時間：11:00〜19:00 休館日：火曜

4. 「Machines of Loving Grace」（KARIMOKU RESEARCH CENTER）

木工とAIの協働から生まれる、新たなインスタレーション

メディアアーティストの真鍋大度とデザインエンジニアの神山友輔が、カリモク家具の木工技術と AI を組み合わせた新作インスタレーションを発表する。Anthropicの共同創業者兼CEOダリオ・アモデイが2024年に発表したエッセイをタイトルの起源に、本展はAIを人間の営みに関わるパートナーとして捉える考えを、木工という具体的なものづくりの現場に置き換えて検討する。

真鍋大度の《Timber / Timbre》は、家具と楽器の関係に着目した作品で、木製筐体にモジュラーシンセサイザーを組み込み、その構成をAI「Claude」とともに探索。植物の生体電位や会場環境の変化も音に取り込む。一方、神山友輔の《Dance as Waves》では、木製の3つの構造体が光をともしたアームを動かすキネティック・インスタレーションが展開される。2階では、作品の制作プロセスとカリモク家具の技術アーカイブも紹介。

「Machines of Loving Grace」 会期：10月17日（土）〜10月25日（日） 場所：KARIMOKU RESEARCH CENTER（東京都港区西麻布2-24-2） 時間：13:00〜18:00 休館日：なし

5. 大友良英＋YCAM 新作展「即興！」（山口情報芸術センター［YCAM］）

音楽と空間から考える、「即興」の可能性

大友良英（1959年生まれ）は、即興演奏を軸に、ノイズ 音楽 や映画音楽など幅広い領域での活動で知られる。サンプリングやフィードバックなどを取り入れた音楽表現に加え、さまざまなアーティストや地域との協働によるプロジェクトにも取り組んできた。本展では、大友の創作における「即興」を軸に、YCAMと複数のアーティストとの共同制作による新作を発表する。

持田敦子 との《Dance》では、解体された木造住宅の柱や梁を組み上げた構造体と、多数のスピーカーや家電から放たれる音を組み合わせる。また、 坂本龍一 へのトリビュート作品《Duo》では、ギターとピアノを物理的な仕組みによって鳴らし、2人の即興演奏を生成する。ほかにも大友＋青山泰知＋伊藤隆之による《without records》などを通して、音楽と空間、複数の作り手の協働から生まれる「即興」のあり方を紹介する。

大友良英＋YCAM 新作展「即興！」 会期：10月17日（土）〜2027年3月1日（月） 場所：山口情報芸術センター［YCAM］（山口県山口市中園町7-7） 時間：10:00〜19:00 休館日：火曜（祝日の場合は翌日）、年末年始（12月29日〜1月3日）

article_text: あざみ野コンテンポラリー vol.17 ニュータウン、インターフェアレンス 都市とわたしたちの関係 Azamino Contemporary vol.17 Suburban Interference: Relations with Urban Space 2026年10月10日 – 11月3日 横浜市民ギャラリーあざみ野、神奈川 https://artazamino.jp/ https://artazamino.jp/event/contemporary17 出品作家：石﨑朝子、川、谷山恭子、トランスフィールドスタジオ、中島晴矢、松田修、山口幸士
excerpt_original: 「あざみ野コンテンポラリー」第17回となる本展では、郊外・ニュータウンなどの「都市」や「土地」のイメージをめぐり、人と場所との関係がどのように結ばれ、揺らいできたのかを考える。7組のアーティストによる映像、インスタレーション、絵画、写真など約100点の作品を展示する。 The post あざみ野コンテンポラリー vol.17 ニュータウン、インターフェアレンス 都市とわたしたちの関係 @ 横浜市民ギャラリーあざみ野 first appeared on ART iT（アートイット） .

title_original: The Artsiest Halloween Party in Town
editorial_title_zh: 全城最具艺术气息的万圣节派对
editorial_excerpt_zh: Hyperallergic 充满精神的晚会，对大都会艺术博物馆（The Met）“服装艺术”展的一点异议，以及艺术圈中女艺术家所谓的“全盛期”究竟是什么？

"heading", "text": "全城最具艺术气息的万圣节派对", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hyperallergic 充满精神的晚会，对大都会艺术博物馆（The Met）“服装艺术”展的一点异议，以及艺术圈中女艺术家所谓的“全盛期”究竟是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "哇……10月转瞬即逝，对吧？万圣节和亡灵节（Día de Muertos）即将到来，但它们只是真正惊悚之夜——11月3日——的热身。也许我们可以用一次博物馆之旅作为小小的慰藉，来为我们的公民职责增添一点甜。马姆达尼市长在大都会艺术博物馆投了票，这里是作为中期选举投票站的少数文化机构之一。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "🦇 回到万圣节 🦇 明天晚上我将在 Hyperallergic 的万圣节派对上见到不少朋友！现场将举行前卫的艺术服装比赛、畅饮酒水以及一些狂欢活动，千万不要错过。你可以在下方找到派对门票以确保入场！对于无法出席的朋友，我们将分享服装比赛的照片来缓解你的 FOMO（错失恐惧症）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "虽然说唱歌手 Kid Cudi 还没有回复我们怪异晚会的 RSVP，但他将身着盛装，主演一部关于已故标志性艺术家让-米歇尔·巴斯奎特（Jean-Michel Basquiat）及其在 80 年代纽约市成名历程的即将上映的传记片《JEAN》。制作工作定于明年开始，但目前我们所知道的仅此而已。同样在服装的话题上，撰稿人娜塔莉·哈达德（Natalie Haddad）发现，大都会艺术博物馆的“服装艺术”展览在理论和实践上都未达预期。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "保持紧扣时事——本周，Powerhouse Arts 与来自墨西哥的 Mestiz Studio 的工匠合作，在曼哈顿熨斗大厦（Flatiron）的北广场搭建了一个巨大的祭坛（ofrenda），以纪念亡灵节。在我们砥砺前行并为子孙后代的福祉投票之际，这是一个多么独特的缅怀和纪念我们祖先及亲人的机会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本周也是你在周六展览闭幕前，去翠贝卡（Tribeca）的马克·施特劳斯画廊（Marc Straus Gallery）欣赏《你生命的全盛期》（The Prime of Your Life）的最后机会。该展汇集了 18 位 75 岁及以上的女艺术家，既是对玛丽莲·明特（Marilyn Minter）名言“艺术界喜欢年轻的坏小子和老太太”的体现，也是一种沉思。策展人兼撰稿人莉亚·特里普レット·哈灵顿（Leah Triplett Harrington）在评论中深入探讨了这一展览，质疑了女性艺术家“全盛期”的界定，尤其是“为什么她们的作品最有可能在晚年才被市场和博物馆赋予价值”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大家万圣节快乐！还有，记得用牙线清理牙齿 :)", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", article_text:
New York Newsletter

The Artsiest Halloween Party in Town

Hyperallergic’s spirited soirée, a bone to pick with “Costume Art” at The Met, and what’s a woman artist’s “prime” in the art world?

Wow…October came and went , didn’t it? Halloween and Día de Muertos are about to turn the corner, but they’re primers for the real fright night — November 3. Maybe we can sugarcoat our civic duty with a trip to the museum as a little treat. Mayor Mamdani cast his vote at The Met, which is one of a handful of cultural institutions serving as polling sites for the midterm elections.

🦇 Back to Halloween 🦇 I’ll be seeing quite a few of you tomorrow evening at Hyperallergic’s Halloween party! There’s going to be an arts-forward costume contest, an open bar, and some general debauchery, so don’t miss out. You can find party tickets to secure your entry below! For those who can’t attend, we’ll be sharing photos from the costume contest to assuage your FOMO.

Though he hasn’t RSVP’d to our spooky soirée, rapper Kid Cudi is putting on a costume as he’s set to star in JEAN , a forthcoming biopic on late iconic artist Jean-Michel Basquiat and his rise to fame during the ‘80s in New York City. Production is set to begin next year, but that’s all we really know for now. Also on the topic of costumes, contributor Natalie Haddad found that The Met’s Costume Art exhibition missed the mark both in theory and in practice.

Keeping things topical — Powerhouse Arts has partnered with artisans from the Mexico-based Mestiz Studio to bring an enormous ofrenda to the Flatiron’s North Plaza in Manhattan this week in observance of Día de Muertos. What a unique opportunity to remember and honor our ancestors and loved ones as we push forward and vote for the well-being of our future generations.

This week is also your last chance to catch The Prime of Your Life at Marc Straus Gallery in Tribeca before it closes on Saturday. Featuring 18 women artists ages 75 and up, the exhibition is both a manifestation and a contemplation of Marilyn Minter’s adage that the “art world loves young bad boys and old ladies.” Curator and contributor Leah Triplett Harrington digs into the exhibition in a review, questioning the identification of a woman artist’s “prime,” especially “when their work is most likely to be valorized by the market and museums only in their older age.”

Happy Halloween, everyone! And remember to floss :)

A Hyperallergic Halloween Party!

Join us on October 28 in Brooklyn, NY for an evening of spooky cocktails, devilish delights, an art-themed costume contest, and more.

RSVP today

Leah Triplett Harrington

The Prime of Your Life at Marc Straus Gallery

"With only their age assembling them, the works in this exhibition offer less of a generational statement and more a critical question of 21st-century feminist art history: What does “prime” mean for a woman artist, when their work is most likely to be valorized by the market and museums only in their older age?"

Lakshmi Rivera Amin

Savdie / Soutine at Norr Cohan

"If Chaïm Soutine hangs up carcasses to dry, Ilana Savdie dissects them with surgical precision...The two artists guide us through the chambers of our own minds and bodies here, as fragmented and estranged as the world around us, and offer glimpses of the freedom we might find in succumbing to their contradictions." Read the full review

Eliza Swann

Conduits of the Unseen: Women Artists Imagine Other Worlds at Andrew Edlin Gallery

"Amid the growing popularity of occult-themed exhibitions, this [exhibition] stands out by asking what esoteric art can make possible, foregrounding its power to challenge entrenched social hierarchies.

...Conduits of the Unseen restores mediumistic work’s social responsibility, emphasizing its aim to serve something beyond the self."

Natalie Haddad

Costume Art at The Metropolitan Museum of Art

"For an exhibition with such a simple title, [this exhibition] is awfully confusing. It’s also fairly problematic, but let’s start with the confusing parts."

Dan Schindel

Suicide Note by Fred Camper

"There is a specific feeling, easy to recognize emotionally but hard to elucidate in words, about trying to power through the numbness of depression to simply live your everyday life. I’m writing these words amidst such a period.

Artist, filmmaker, and critic Fred Camper sought to capture that feeling with Suicide Note , which he describes as 'born out of an intense personal despair, and a desire to depict a failure of the self.'"

Martha Wilson

The Perfect Moment: God, Sex, Art, and the Birth of America’s Culture Wars (2026 ) by Isaac Butler

"Butler has done the research. I recommend this book without reservation because it is a thorough, accurate account of a fraught time in American history, when artists were motivated to take action to ensure that their freedom of expression is preserved — just like the present moment.'"

Upcoming deadline for MFA program applications at University at Buffalo

Learn more

News

Several museums open their doors for early voters , including the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani cast his ballot.

Designed by artisans from Mestiz Studio in Mexico, an enormous ofrenda titled “Twenty Petal Flower” begins to blossom in Manhattan, six days before the start of Día de Muertos.

Kid Cudi announces his hand in writing, directing, and starring in the forthcoming project JEAN, a biopic of late contemporary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat .

Multidisciplinary artist Turiya Adkins, artist and curator Timothy Yanick Hunter, and photographer and filmmaker Clifford Prince King have been selected as the Studio Museum’s yearlong artists-in-residence for 2026–27 .

What Else Is Happening?

The annual Canstruction design competition, in which architects, artists, and engineers team up to create monumental sculptures from unopened food cans before they’re donated to City Harvest, returns to Brookfield Place. The live build takes place on Thursday, but the sculptures will remain on display till November 9. (Thu, 10/29) [ bfplny.org ]

Pigeon lovers, step aside — it’s the city rat’s turn for the limelight. In the spirit of the rat race, Rats in the City isn’t just a rodent appreciation event; it’s a costume competition. The event closes out the Data Vandals and Archtober collaboration at the newsstand on the downtown 6 train platform at East 51st Street and Lexington. Bring your own pizza. (Fri, Oct 30) [ aiany.org ]

Socrates Sculpture Park is hosting its annual Halloween Harvest Festival with workshops led by local artists, a canine costume contest, a crash course on the city’s bat species, and a vegan food market. (Sat, Oct 31) [ socratessculpturepark.org ]

Halloween? More like Meowloween … Catbaret is a feline-inclined variety show of comedy, live music, burlesque, related raffle prizes with proceeds benefiting Rescue NYC, and a free pair of cat ears for each guest. (Sat, Oct 31) [ caveat.nyc ]

In anticipation of the midterm elections, the Button Boys and Indoor Recess are hosting a democracy-themed button-making event at A.MANO Brooklyn. Don’t worry, magnets are also an option. (Sun, Nov 1) [ luma.com ]

Writer Allison C. Meier is leading a class on funerary art through deciphering cemetery symbols. Translate parting messages from generations of late New Yorkers resting in burial grounds across all five boroughs. (Sun, Nov 1) [ eventbrite.com ]

Painter Eric Aho celebrates the publication of the first comprehensive monograph of his landscape works. Hyperallergic ’s veteran critic John Yau joins Aho at Rizzoli Bookstore for a conversation on the new book, which covers four decades of the artist’s practice. (Mon, Nov 2) [ eventbrite.com ]

Rogers）表示。“《直面》为参观者带来令人振奋的视觉体验，架起了时尚与艺术世界的桥梁，而《英国皇室肖像》则展现了英国皇室更具个人色彩的一面。”特斯蒂诺亲自为这些展览挑选了作品。展出的照片回顾了他多产的职业生涯，该生涯始于特斯蒂诺于1976年从他的祖国秘鲁来到伦敦后不久。《直面》汲取了数千张精心造型的影像，记录了他在追求并礼赞美丽之途中的创作历程。特斯蒂诺的照片大胆、富有图形感且“直面观者”。展览展现了时尚、优雅、性与裸露，反映了这位摄影师独特的审美与风格跨度。", article_text:
Archives – October 23, 2012

Mario Testino ’s compelling fashion and celebrity photographs have appeared in international magazines and advertising campaigns for leading fashion houses for the past three decades. Beginning October 21, the man behind the camera that has captured countless iconic images for Vogue and Vanity Fair is featured in two exhibitions of his work at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA)— Mario Testino: In Your Face and British Royal Portraits . These exhibitions are his first in the United States.

It showcases 122 images by the photographer, known for works that evoke elegance, beauty, style, irreverence, and contradiction. The range and quality of Testino’s career is illustrated in photographs of international superstars, such as models Kate Moss, Stephanie Seymour, and Gisele Bündchen; actors Nicole Kidman and Gwyneth Paltrow; musicians Mick Jagger, Madonna, and Lady Gaga; and athletes David Beckham and Tom Brady. Mario Testino: British Royal Portraits focuses on the portraits he has taken of generations of the British royal family.

“Mario Testino’s images are full of color, movement, and provocation. He is one of the greatest and most mercurial image-makers of our time, and we are pleased to present the first US exhibitions of his works,” said Malcolm Rogers, Ann and Graham Gund Director of the MFA. “In Your Face offers visitors an exhilarating visual experience, bridging the worlds of fashion and art, while British Royal Portraits presents a more personal look at the British royal family.” Testino has personally chosen the works for these exhibitions. The photographs on view offer a retrospective of his prolific career, which began shortly after Testino’s arrival in London from his native Peru in 1976. In Your Face draws upon thousands of exquisitely styled images that document his creative journey in pursuit—and in celebration—of beauty. Testino’s photographs are bold, graphic, and “in your face.” The exhibition illustrates fashion, elegance, sex, and nudity, reflecting the photographer’s unique aesthetic and stylistic range.

“I am honored to be invited by the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston to exhibit my work in these two exhibitions, my first in the United States,” said Testino. “These exhibitions are a very personal reflection of the past 30 years in which I have been a photographer.”

In Your Face provides access to Testino’s world—from models, movie stars, and musicians, to a host of glitterati. At the entrance to the Gund Gallery, a wall of 16 screens offers behind-the-scenes video of the globetrotting photographer. In addition, visitors to the exhibition can experience Testino in action and recalling career-defining moments on the Museum’s hand-held multimedia guide, which features audio and video selections relating to works in the exhibitions.

Among the many famous faces on view are Jennifer Lopez, Keith Richards, Kate Winslet, and Ashton Kutcher. Styled portraits are juxtaposed with candid private party snapshots, nudes with fashion, black-and-white with color, and interiors with exterior settings. These arrangements capture the interplay of mass media, celebrity, and glamour, in an installation that offers the observer a more intimate connection with the works. The photographs, many of them printed on aluminum, rest on shelves running the length of the teal-colored Gund Gallery. Images vary in size, ranging from monumental color prints (8’ x 6’) to intimately sized (1’ x 2’) black-and-white snapshots.

“The MFA’s relationship with Mario Testino began when he came to the Museum in 2010 to participate in the Karsh photography lecture series” said Anne Havinga, Estrellita and Yousuf Karsh Senior Curator of Photographs at the MFA. “These two exhibitions are the result of a wonderful collaboration between Mario and the Museum, and reveal the artist’s perspective on the popular culture of our time.”

Testino is highly regarded for the photographs of British royalty he has been commissioned to take throughout his career, and he has chosen his personal favorites for the exhibition British Royal Portraits. “I have been so fortunate to have documented key moments in the lives of the British royal family. I have always been inspired by their sense of tradition and duty—it is always a huge honor for me to photograph them and I am delighted that many of these pictures will be on display, together for the first time, in the Herb Ritts gallery at the MFA,” said Testino.

British Royal Portraits is the first US showing the 2010 engagement portraits Testino was commissioned to take of Prince William and Kate Middleton, now TRH The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. Also on view is the iconic and elegant black-and-white portrait he took of Diana, Princess of Wales, which first appeared in Vanity Fair magazine in 1997 and was her last official sitting before her death that year. The framed images of the royals—many measuring approximately 3’ x 4‘—are shown against royal blue walls. They range from a snapshot of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II to informal black-and-white images of Prince Charles with his sons William and Harry. Also on view is the first picture Testino took of members of the House of Windsor a few years after arriving in London from Peru. The photographer snapped an impromptu black-and-white shot of The Queen Mother and her grandson, Prince Edward, as they passed by crowds gathered in London’s streets to celebrate the marriage of HRH The Prince of Wales and Lady Diana Spencer in 1981. Since then, Testino has become a preferred photographer of the royal family.

Gilles Decamps

Mario Testino: In Your Face From October 21, 2012 to February 3, 2013 Museum of Fine Arts, Boston Avenue of the Arts 465 Huntington Avenue Boston, Massachusetts 02115 General Information: 617-267-9300

article_text:
“The art of theater is a voyage,” wrote François Regnault, before adding: “Motionless in the middle of the city.” The line opens Navire amiral as an epigraph, set down like a compass on the chart table. It would suit the house of Molière, whose vocabulary still smells of hemp and tar: lines, pulleys, tackles, canvas. Few people know it, but in the days when sailors stayed ashore through the winter, theaters hired them to work the stage machinery. The sailors left, but their knots remained.

Stéphane Lavoué spent ten years inside this windowless hull. As associate artist at the Comédie-Française from 2015 to 2025, during Éric Ruf’s tenure, he grew steadily drawn to the trades of the shadows: stagehands, prop masters, costume makers, all those who keep the show running and never take a bow. Long days under artificial light, in the understage and the workshops. “I sometimes felt as if I were moving around inside a submarine,” he recalls. A mere image? A lead, rather. “As early as the 16th century, theater borrowed heavily from sailing ships, taking their techniques and their vocabulary,” the artist explains, and today’s stagehands “often see themselves as crew members.” Hence the journey in reverse: leaving the fly tower for the gangways, the Salle Richelieu for the Royale, as the French Navy is nicknamed.

Three vessels, and three closed worlds. The multi-mission frigate Bretagne , in the Iroise Sea. The nuclear ballistic missile submarine Le Téméraire , somewhere in the North Atlantic. The aircraft carrier Charles de Gaulle , in the western Mediterranean. There, Stéphane Lavoué found “the same rituals, the same precision of gesture, the same need to act as one body to accomplish a shared mission.” The anaphora is a gift, so we keep it. A difficult parallel? Very. So the photographer shuffles the cards, and the book becomes a third country, its borders erased.

The captions wait at the end, gathered together, and as precise as a ship’s log. “This loss of bearings is deliberate,” Stéphane acknowledges. “It lets readers project their own stories onto the images.” Until then, everyone navigates by dead reckoning. A wig on its stand, as demure as a figurehead (Comédie-Française, 2024). Casts of actors’ faces stored in the basement of the Salle Richelieu, a gallery of plaster ancestors. A fake porthole stuck to the wall of the Bretagne ‘s cafeteria, on a 142-meter frigate with only one real porthole, in the commander’s office. An aquarium in the commanding officer’s wardroom aboard Le Téméraire , where the two crews, red and blue, share responsibility for keeping the fish alive.

For Stéphane Lavoué, the most powerful experience remains the submarine. “I often compare it to a trip to the Moon,” he says. “Once you’re submerged, you lose all direct connection with the outside world. You no longer know whether you’re moving forward or backward, whether it’s day or night.” Captain Nemo is not far off, library included: the one aboard Le Téméraire holds, according to the caption, the complete run of the manga The Summit of the Gods (every era has its classics). A nuclear power plant able to vanish beneath the sea for months, a crew of 110 sailors, an infirmary that turns into an operating room: a true science-fiction set.

Portraiture remains the keel of Stéphane Lavoué’s work, the man who, from Zinedine Zidane to Salman Rushdie, has photographed just about every public face France has to offer. “I didn’t just want to show professionals at work. I was trying to bring characters to the surface,” the artist says. Hence Lieutenant Julien, a Rafale fighter pilot in the ready room. Or Sébastien, known as “the Thigh,” the head chef who serves 230 meals a day in a kitchen of two square meters. Or Thomas, known as “the Sorcerer,” a nurse and radiology operator. Corsairs’ nicknames. On the theater side, Lino, César and Kevin, stagehands, and Hinda, who presses the ruffs and starched collars.

There remains the second captain. Éric Ruf, honorary sociétaire of the Comédie-Française and self-described “stage sailor,” contributes fragments attributed to fictional authors, drawn from fictional novels: Le Retour à Narvik (The Return to Narvik) by Knut Eleisson, Augustin le capiste (Augustin from Cap-Sizun) by Nolwenn Legars, Mon père ne m’a pas aimé (My Father Didn’t Love Me) by Sylvain Touzé (an unbeatable title). In them, a Norwegian pastor and a German captain dine in the middle of the Atlantic on April 10, 1940; a child surrounded by pirates finds, at the bottom of a chest, a single mauve satin slipper (Claudel, whose The Satin Slipper is rehearsed in the pages of the book, would approve); Jonah discovers, in the belly of the whale, that he has company. An anonymous treatise even claims that the red of Italian-style theater curtains comes from a room aboard warships, painted red so as not to frighten the wounded who were amputated there, and called “the theater.” True? False? A gangway legend. “His texts don’t explain the images; they shift them,” Stéphane Lavoué sums up. “The book works the same way,” he continues. “It deliberately sustains a degree of uncertainty and fiction.”

Born in Mulhouse in 1976, Stéphane Lavoué graduated from the École supérieure du bois, a school of wood engineering, and spent two years in the Brazilian Amazon buying timber for an industrial group before changing course in 2001. Winner of the Prix Niépce in 2018, and in 2022 one of the laureates of the major photographic commission “La France sous leurs yeux” (France Through Their Eyes), for which he photographed young army recruits, he showed Navire amiral at the Ateliers des Capucins in Brest from June 12 to September 20, 2026. The book, for its part, holds its course. And if you ask Stéphane Lavoué which image sums up the whole, he points to a corridor at the Comédie-Française, “a perspective that sinks into darkness toward an almost invisible vanishing point.” And he adds: “When I took it, I immediately thought of a submarine.”

Navire amiral by Stéphane Lavoué, with texts by Éric Ruf, is published by Atelier EXB and available for €49.

title_original: Kim Jung-hoon, Roh Jeong-eui and Show Kasamatsu on genre and cross-cultural collaboration in “Shaving”
editorial_title_zh: 金荣勋、卢正义与笠松将谈论《Shaving》中的类型片元素与跨文化合作
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在第31届釜山国际电影节竞赛单元展映

"paragraph", "text": "金荣勋凭借其长片处女作《Tinker Ticker》（2013）崭露头角，该片曾入围东京国际电影节“亚洲未来”单元。十多年后，他携恐怖惊悚片《Shaving》回归，该片剧本由洪成润和卢道贤共同执笔，入围了釜山国际电影节竞赛单元。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "借着电影《Shaving》展映之际，导演金荣勋与两位主演卢正义、笠松将畅谈了该项目的缘起、类型的融合、角色在体力与情感上的挑战，以及片中韩语与日语交织的拍摄体验。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "《Shaving》正在釜山国际电影节展映", "links": [{"text": "Busan International "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "刮胡子这一行为成为了推动电影核心事件的催化剂。这个项目是如何开始的？刮胡子在片中又起到了什么作用？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我是大约在去年6月份收到剧本的。它由两位编剧洪成润和卢道贤共同创作，他们是学生时代的老朋友。据我了解，当时他们正在合作，有一天男编剧去女编剧家开会。因为他们认识太久了，洪成润那天工作太忙，连胡子都没刮。她拿他的胡茬开玩笑，让他去刮胡子。他们找到了一个属于卢道贤前男友的剃须刀，最后他竟然真的用了。大概进行到一半时，他们突然迸发灵感，项目就这样开始了，我是这么听说的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从我拿到剧本的那天起，直到电影杀青，我一直在思考“刮胡子”意味着什么。对于男人来说，这是日常生活的一部分，是每天都会做的事。但如果你停下来想一想，剃须刀其实也很危险，甚至令人发冷。我们的电影从一对情侣看似平凡的生活切入，随后危险逐步升级，我觉得这与这个概念完美契合。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在参与这部电影的过程中，你觉得最享受的是什么？最想尝试的又是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卢正义：动作戏对我来说是一个全新的类型，也是我第一次尝试，所以关于它的一切都既刺激又有趣，拍摄的每一天我都乐在其中。我们一起排练动作设计，互相照顾，并深入讨论了如何尽可能展现出每个角色和每种处境。这是一次新鲜的挑战，也是一段非常快乐的经历，我想这会成为一段美好的回忆。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "笠松将：我从来没拍过这样的作品。刚拿到这个项目时，有人跟我说这是一部爱情片。我并不是一个经常演爱情片的演员。我演的大多是反派和黑暗、具有威胁性的角色，所以大家开玩笑说：“哦，现在演爱情片啦！”但拍完这部电影后，我觉得这是一种更深沉的爱情。片中简单、表层的爱情也很重要，我希望观众会喜欢。但老实说，对我而言，这是一部根植于一个年轻女性的痛苦与挣扎之中的爱情片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种类型片的融合是剧本中原本就有的，还是你有意融入了自己喜爱的多种类型元素？你为什么会选择这种混合的方法？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "金荣勋：你所描述的绝大部分类型框架在剧本里就已经存在了。有些元素（比如那个生物）在改编过程中发生了一些变化。我第一次读剧本时，正是这些东西最吸引我。难点在于如何在不失整部电影连贯性的前提下，以丰富而新鲜的方式呈现它们，最重要的是如何顺着主角的情感轨迹，让所有元素在结尾汇聚到一起。这对我来说是最重要的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影极大地依赖演员的实力，在如此局促的空间内搭档演出一定不容易。为了找到彼此的默契，你们在片场和排练时都聊了些什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Show Kasamatsu：开拍前，我和导演进行了深入的交流。对我来说最重要的是：观众能否确信他们看到的这个人就是他表面上看起来的那样？他们真的能知道这个男人是谁吗？我和导演以及搭档就此进行了大量讨论。在我的戏份中，她对我的举动做出了回应和反应，我们一点点构建起表演。我希望观众在观看时也能带着“这个男人是谁？”的疑问去享受电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卢正如：正如Show所说，主角最爱、最信任的人变成了她最不信任的人，她的生活也从幸福跌入了噩梦。为了刻画这段心路历程，我们在拍摄期间需要进行大量的交流。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在动作戏拍摄期间，多亏了我们优秀的导演和身边的演员同仁，我们感到很有安全感，并且就如何更充分地表达情感交流了许多意见。而我的角色素妍和所有人一样，背负着创伤。直面这些创伤并重塑生活，正是她故事的核心。在与搭档的排练中，我们尝试了许多不同的方法，包括大量的即兴发挥，以此来丰富电影的细节。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "金导演，请分享一下选择卢正义和笠松将的幕后动机", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "先从卢正义说起。我很久以前就注意到她了，当时她作为年轻演员参演了同一家制作公司的一部电影。她来试镜并被选中，我关注了该片的制作及上映全过程，觉得她是一位非常迷人的演员。此后我在不同的作品中不断看到她，觉得她成长得很好。在读这个剧本时，我觉得她能展现出观众在她身上未曾见过的面貌。她一直以来都很可爱、开朗、讨人喜欢，但我相信她也能表现出更具反应性、更脆弱的一面，而且她会非常契合这个角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "至于笠松将，我最初是在我深为尊敬的迈克尔·曼（Michael Mann）的《东京罪恶》（Tokyo Vice）中看到他的。我被他深深吸引了。后来我们的制作公司 Star Platinum 邀请他出演了《好消息》（Good News）(2025)，而在我们选角期间，他的名字再次被提起。在最初的剧本中，这对情侣是异地恋，既然他们是在时隔很久之后重逢，我就想，干脆把他设定为外国人或许行得通。这样一来，前男友和现男友之间的区别就会更加鲜明，而当日常相伴的男友突然发生转变时，那种不安感和疏离感也可以通过在韩语和日语之间切换来加剧。这似乎是个好主意，于是我就向他发出了邀约。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "两位演员对这次合作有何感受？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卢正义：对我来说，笠松将是一位我仰慕的前辈，是人生路上走在我前面的人，我真心觉得他非常了不起。我常常琢磨，自己能否像他那样去海外发展并展现实力。看到他让我意识到自己还很年轻，还有很大的成长空间。我希望他能继续在韩国拍摄更多电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "笠松将：我也一直在这么说，而且我会把更多的项目带到韩国。让我惊讶的是拍摄期间有多冷。韩国太冷了！", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "韩语和日语之间的来回切换赋予了这部电影一种重要的微妙语感。在剧本中，我的台词全部都是韩语。我努力学习并完成了表演，但发音确实是一场苦战。导演和团队帮了我很多，我们一起商讨并自然地决定：“这里说日语更好，那里说韩语更好。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "卢正义：当笠松将用日语即兴发挥时，即便我并非完全听懂那些词句，也能确切感受到其中的语感。这让人感到非常恐惧，甚至更加不寒而栗。在表演时，我不断感到迷茫：这是那个真正爱我的男友在说话，还是我的噩梦又要重新开始了？韩语和日语听上去如此不同，有着如此微妙的效果，我想笠松将在选择这些即兴台词时一定非常用心。我希望观众也能留意到这一点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "笠松先生，作为一位现在已经在两个国家都工作过的演员，您如何看待在韩国与在日本拍戏的区别，您对韩国电影又有何感受？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Kim Jung-hoon, Roh Jeong-eui and Show Kasamatsu on genre and cross-cultural collaboration in “Shaving”

Presenting in the competition section at the 31st Busan International Film Festival

Kim Jung-hoon gained recognition with his debut feature “Tinker Ticker” (2013), which competed in the Asian Future section of the Tokyo International Film Festival. More than a decade later, he returns with “Shaving”, a horror-thriller based on a screenplay by Hong Seong-yoon and Roh Dohyeon, presented in the competition section of the Busan International Film Festival.

On the occasion of his film “Shaving”, director Kim Jung-hoon and his two leads, Roh Jeong-eui and Show Kasamatsu, talked about how the project began, the blend of genres, the physical and emotional demands of the roles, and the interplay of Korean and Japanese on set.

Shaving is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The act of shaving becomes the catalyst for the film’s central events. How did the project begin, and what role does shaving play in the film?

I received the script around June last year. It was written by two screenwriters, Hong Seong-yoon and Roh Dohyeon, who are close friends from schooldays. As I understand it, they were working together, and one day the male writer went to the female writer’s home for a meeting. Since they have known each other for so long, Hong hadn’t shaved that day because he’d been busy working. She teased him about his stubble and told him to go and shave. They found a razor that had belonged to Roh’s ex-boyfriend, and he actually ended up using it. About halfway through, an idea struck them, and that is how the project began, or so I was told.

From the moment I received the script to the day the film was finished, I kept thinking about what shaving means. For men it is an everyday routine, something done daily. But if you stop and think about it, a razor can also be dangerous, even chilling. Our film begins with what looks like the ordinary life of a couple and grows steadily more dangerous, and I felt that fit the concept perfectly.

What did you enjoy most while working on the film, and what did you most want to try?

Roh Jeong-eui: Action was a new genre for me, and the first time I had tried it, so everything about it was exciting and fun, and I enjoyed every day of shooting. We rehearsed the choreography together, looked after one another, and talked a lot about how to bring out each character and each situation as well as we could. It was a fresh challenge and a really happy experience, and I think it will remain a good memory.

Show Kasamatsu: I had never done anything quite like this. When I first received the project, I was told it was a romance. I’m not an actor who does much romance. I’ve mostly played villains and dark, menacing characters, so people teased me, saying, “So it’s a romance now!” But after we shot the film, I felt it was a much deeper kind of romance. The simpler, surface-level romance matters in the film too, and I hope audiences enjoy it. But to me, honestly, it is a romance rooted in the pain and struggles of one young woman.

Was the genre mix already there in the screenplay, or did you deliberately bring in elements of the many genres you love? Why did you choose such a hybrid approach?

Kim Jung-hoon : Most of the genre framework you describe was already in the screenplay. Some elements, such as the creature, changed during the adaptation. When I first read the script, those were exactly the things that attracted me most. The challenge was how to present them in a rich and fresh way without losing the coherence of the whole film, and above all how to follow the protagonist’s emotional journey so that everything comes together at the end. That was the most important thing for me.

This film depends heavily on the strength of its actors, and working in tandem within such a confined setting can’t have been easy. What did you talk about on set and in rehearsals to find your rhythm together?

Show Kasamatsu: Before shooting began, I talked at length with the director. What mattered most to me was this: can the audience be sure that the person they are watching is who he appears to be? Can they ever really know who this man is? I discussed that a great deal with the director and with my co-star. In my scenes, she responded and reacted to what I was doing, and we built the performance up bit by bit. I hope viewers will enjoy asking themselves, “Who is this man?” as they watch.

Roh Jeong-eui: As Show said, the person the protagonist loves and trusts most becomes the person she can trust least, and she goes from happiness to nightmare. We needed to talk a great deal during filming to portray that journey.

During the action scenes, thanks to our wonderful director and the fellow actors around us, we felt secure, and we exchanged many ideas about how to express the emotions more fully. And my character, So-yeon, like anyone, carries trauma. Confronting that trauma and rebuilding her life is at the heart of her story. In rehearsals with my co-stars we tried many different approaches, including a lot of improvisation, in an effort to enrich the details of the film.

Director Kim, please share the motivation behind choosing Roh Jeong-eui and Show Kasamatsu

Let me start with Roh Jeong-eui. I first came across her a long time ago, when she was cast as a young actress in a film from the same production company. She came in to audition, she was cast, and I followed her through the making of the film and its release, and I thought she was a very appealing actress. I kept seeing her in different projects after that and felt she was growing well. While reading this script, I felt that she could bring out sides that audiences hadn’t seen from her. She has always been cute, bright and lovable, but I believed she could also express a more reactive, more vulnerable side, and that she would be a wonderful fit.

As for Show Kasamatsu, I first saw him in Michael Mann’s “Tokyo Vice”, whom I deeply respect. I was captivated. Then our production company, Star Platinum, cast him in “Good News” (2025), and his name came up again around the time we were casting. In the original screenplay the couple is in a long-distance relationship, and since they are meeting again after a long time, I thought it might work to make him foreign altogether. That would make the difference between the ex-boyfriend and the current boyfriend much clearer, and the unease and sense of alienation when an everyday boyfriend suddenly transforms could be heightened by shifting between Korean and Japanese. It seemed like a good idea, so I proposed the role to him.

How did the two actors feel about working together?

Roh Jeong-eui: To me, Show is a senior I look up to, someone ahead of me in life, and I truly feel he is remarkable. I often wondered whether I could go abroad and show my abilities as he has done. Seeing him made me realize how young I still am and how much room I have to grow. I hope he will keep making many films in Korea.

Show Kasamatsu: I keep saying that too, and I’ll be bringing more projects to Korea. What surprised me was how cold it was during the shoot. Korea is so cold!

The back-and-forth between Korean and Japanese gives this film an important nuance. In the script, all of my lines were in Korean. I studied hard and performed them, but pronunciation was a real struggle. The director and the team helped me a great deal, and we worked together to decide naturally, “Here Japanese is better, here Korean is better.”

Roh Jeong-eui: When Show improvised in Japanese, even if I didn’t fully understand the words, I could feel exactly what the nuance was. That made it very frightening and even more chilling. As I performed, I kept being confused: is this the boyfriend who truly loves me speaking, or is my nightmare starting all over again? Korean and Japanese sound so different, with such a subtle effect, and I think Show chose his ad-libs with great care. I hope audiences will look out for that as well.

Mr. Kasamatsu, as an actor who has now worked in both countries, how do you see the differences between filming in Korea and in Japan, and how do you feel about Korean films?

There is a difference in the shooting systems. I believe Korea is stricter about protecting actors’ working conditions. Japan is working hard on this, but it isn’t perfect yet. There is also a difference in creative approach. The impression I have is that Korea sets out to make a miracle happen in front of the camera. To do that, everything is carefully built, from the atmosphere to the costumes, the makeup and the direction. But if every image is constructed too tightly, there can be moments when the actors’ energy drops.

In Japan, good films, good dramas, good actors and directors wait for a miracle and make it happen on set. So the temperature is different, but I wouldn’t say one is better or worse. I enjoy both, and I want to keep learning in Korea and in Japan from wonderful actors in each.

article_text:
Sylvester Stallone is opening up about how decades of daredevilry have affected him—and why he considers himself an “idiot” for continuing to do his own stunts year after year.

In a recent interview with Fox News Digital , the “Rocky” actor said he has “millions, millions of regrets” about his action career. “I could literally spend a half hour talking about injuries, the amount, not even like one, I’m talking about 30 hours, 30 minutes of just individual ones, because it becomes compounded. I have been injured many, many times, but after ‘Expendables,’ I ended up with nine back operations, three neck fusions. Both shoulders ripped out, eye, you know, all kinds of lens put … it’s been brutal,” he said, adding that he’s never been “quite the same” since the surgeries.

Related Stories

'Bob's Burgers' Sets Holiday Hulu Special Release Date, Teases First Look at NYCC

'Dungeon Crawler Carl' Live-Action TV Series to Begin Shooting in 2027, More Details Coming 'Very Soon'

Stallone starred in — and also directed — the action thriller “The Expendables” in 2010 alongside Jason Statham, Mickey Rourke and more. While filming a scene where Stallone got tackled by WWE legend Steve Austin, the stunt went wrong and left Stallone with dislocated shoulders and a fractured neck that required more than seven back surgeries. The “Rambo” actor needed a metal plate inserted into his neck and spinal fusions.

Stallone’s moral of the story is to “let other people do their job.” “Don’t be a stage hawk, or whatever you call it, a showboat. I know a lot of people are thinking about doing stunts … don’t. Don’t. Let the pro do it,” Stallone said. “You cannot beat gravity; when you hit the ground, you lose, and it’s going to come back.”

He continued, “I mean, just ask every football player in the world. So yeah, and people go, ‘Aren’t you proud of them?’ No. I think I’m an idiot for doing that. I’m proud that I broke myself in pieces. Like, duh, no.”

The actor shared a similar piece of advice ahead of the release of his memoir, “The Steps,” last month; Stallone told The New York Times that treating his body in the “masochistic” ways he did came “at a terrible price.” “If I could do it over again, I would say, ‘Let someone else carry the banner and don’t do your own stunts.”

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在第八届 T3 摄影节上，这场节日放慢了日本首都匆忙的步伐，将摄影塑造为连接不同世界的中间人。在城市的墙壁上，18 位艺术家打破边界、声讨边界，或画出新的边界，将那些我们往往分离开的事物凝聚在一起。一场……

To reach skyscraper lobbies, building gables, or a café-gallery, he takes the neighborhood’s historic backstreets rather than its broad avenues. On these walls and facades, 18 artists from Japan and abroad are on view for 24 days, free of charge."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Reconnecting with the history of the place, to “forge an identity and bring life to it,” in the words of T3’s creator: the event’s commitment echoes this year’s minimal, inspired theme, “と” (to), meaning “and.” “It is a coordinating conjunction that sets things against each other but also brings them together,” Ihiro Hayami explains. “We wanted to reflect on the duality this word implies, as another way of thinking about the world, modeled on the self-portraits take over the vast glass hall of the Midtown Yaesu complex. There is no escaping this gaze, which forces a face-to-face encounter, eye to eye. In the exhibition “When Things Become a Crown,” Zanele Muholi, a leading figure of visual activism in South Africa, blends opposites by staging these carefully dressed reflections of the self. Clothespins and safety pins, paper rolls and rubber gloves were the tools of alienation of Muholi’s mother, a domestic worker employed by a white family under apartheid. Muholi wears them to reclaim their history, their origins, their identity, and to denounce the discrimination experienced by Black communities past and present, down to the way they are represented, a convention the artist plays with. Pushed to extreme contrast, these monochrome images celebrate Muholi’s Africanness and the color of their skin, long poorly rendered by film stock calibrated for white skin, and the target of racist practices such as the “pencil test”: a pencil pushed into the hair was used to assign racial classifications under apartheid, which the artist’s headdress of combs subtly evokes."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/t3-2026-zanele-muholi-1.jpg", "alt": "Self-portrait of Zanele Muholi wearing a headdress of toilet paper rolls, arms raised, in black and white", "caption": "© Zanele Muholi, courtesy of T3 Photo Festival Tokyo 2026", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.blind-magazine.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/t3-2026-zanele-muholi-2.jpg", "alt": "Self-portrait of Zanele Muholi with a metal funnel and a round object covering the face, in black and white", "caption": "© Zanele Muholi, courtesy of T3 Photo Festival Tokyo 2026", "credit": "Blind Magazine"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "What images say"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A short distance away, on the walls of a café-gallery in the neighboring Kyobashi district, the exhibition “Trace and Vision” showcases the work of Japanese photographer Sayaka Uehara. A recipient of the prize awarded by the town of Higashikawa, on the island of Hokkaido, home to an international photography festival every summer, the artist sheds light on the darker side of her native archipelago, Okinawa, held captive by the idealized images that cling to it: paradise beaches and lush landscapes. “To reflect on the problems facing Okinawa (…), I had to go beyond simply observing its landscapes,” the artist says. Far from these postcard views, her images capture a seemingly ordinary daily life: a backyard, a wrinkled hand, a waiting room where time seems to have stood still."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Each of Sayaka Uehara’s images forms a complex mosaic, studded with rough edges, that maps Okinawa’s many layers. “I believe photography has the power to make visible things that are accessible to everyone, yet neglected, ignored, or forgotten,” the artist continues. The wounds of the colonial past (once the Ryukyu Kingdom, the archipelago was annexed by Japan in 1879), economic inequality, and the overbearing presence of American military bases surface in a scene, a detail: a worn building, Coca-Cola red parasols planted in the sand, a barbershop for soldiers, a Kerama deer crossing an empty street. “When I take the time to look at my photographs, I feel Nozomi Suzuki’s photographs, the second half of this duo exhibition, question our anthropocentrism by drawing attention to the images objects create on their own, “without human intervention or intention,” the artist specifies. The vent in a saucepan lid, a hole nibbled by an insect in a leaf, a tiny cavity in a piece of wood: every opening in our surroundings becomes a chance for the photographer to slip in her device inspired by the camera obscura. Using a lensless wooden camera, she turns these everyday apertures into a way of capturing images and watching the world exist in our absence. “These images usually go unnoticed, blending into the ambient light, but even when we pay no attention, light is constantly creating images,” Nozomi Suzuki tells Blind . “I feel that these invisible images are like monologues whispered by light itself.” What does light say when we let it speak? It answers in its own vocabulary, a multitude of traces, stains, and silhouettes laid down on photosensitive paper. article_text:
The area just west of Tokyo Station, lined with tall office and retail towers, carries a history its facades barely hint at. “This is where the city’s first photo studios were born, where Utagawa Hiroshige (the master of Japanese woodblock prints, editor’s note) spent the last years of his life; it is also where kabuki theater flourished in the Edo period,” Ihiro Hayami, director and founder of the T3 urban photography festival, enthusiastically recounts. To reach skyscraper lobbies, building gables, or a café-gallery, he takes the neighborhood’s historic backstreets rather than its broad avenues. On these walls and facades, 18 artists from Japan and abroad are on view for 24 days, free of charge.

Reconnecting with the history of the place, to “forge an identity and bring life to it,” in the words of T3’s creator: the event’s commitment echoes this year’s minimal, inspired theme, “と” (to), meaning “and.” “It is a coordinating conjunction that sets things against each other but also brings them together,” Ihiro Hayami explains. “We wanted to reflect on the duality this word implies, as another way of thinking about the world, modeled on the Asian philosophy of yin and yang.”

Avenging the affront

Zanele Muholi’s large-format self-portraits take over the vast glass hall of the Midtown Yaesu complex. There is no escaping this gaze, which forces a face-to-face encounter, eye to eye. In the exhibition “When Things Become a Crown,” Zanele Muholi, a leading figure of visual activism in South Africa, blends opposites by staging these carefully dressed reflections of the self. Clothespins and safety pins, paper rolls and rubber gloves were the tools of alienation of Muholi’s mother, a domestic worker employed by a white family under apartheid. Muholi wears them to reclaim their history, their origins, their identity, and to denounce the discrimination experienced by Black communities past and present, down to the way they are represented, a convention the artist plays with. Pushed to extreme contrast, these monochrome images celebrate Muholi’s Africanness and the color of their skin, long poorly rendered by film stock calibrated for white skin, and the target of racist practices such as the “pencil test”: a pencil pushed into the hair was used to assign racial classifications under apartheid, which the artist’s headdress of combs subtly evokes.

What images say

A short distance away, on the walls of a café-gallery in the neighboring Kyobashi district, the exhibition “Trace and Vision” showcases the work of Japanese photographer Sayaka Uehara. A recipient of the prize awarded by the town of Higashikawa, on the island of Hokkaido, home to an international photography festival every summer, the artist sheds light on the darker side of her native archipelago, Okinawa, held captive by the idealized images that cling to it: paradise beaches and lush landscapes. “To reflect on the problems facing Okinawa (…), I had to go beyond simply observing its landscapes,” the artist says. Far from these postcard views, her images capture a seemingly ordinary daily life: a backyard, a wrinkled hand, a waiting room where time seems to have stood still.

Each of Sayaka Uehara’s images forms a complex mosaic, studded with rough edges, that maps Okinawa’s many layers. “I believe photography has the power to make visible things that are accessible to everyone, yet neglected, ignored, or forgotten,” the artist continues. The wounds of the colonial past (once the Ryukyu Kingdom, the archipelago was annexed by Japan in 1879), economic inequality, and the overbearing presence of American military bases surface in a scene, a detail: a worn building, Coca-Cola red parasols planted in the sand, a barbershop for soldiers, a Kerama deer crossing an empty street. “When I take the time to look at my photographs, I feel that every element in them bears witness to something, a small voice that cannot quite be put into words,” she says.

The creative power of light

Shifting the gaze. Nozomi Suzuki’s photographs, the second half of this duo exhibition, question our anthropocentrism by drawing attention to the images objects create on their own, “without human intervention or intention,” the artist specifies. The vent in a saucepan lid, a hole nibbled by an insect in a leaf, a tiny cavity in a piece of wood: every opening in our surroundings becomes a chance for the photographer to slip in her device inspired by the camera obscura. Using a lensless wooden camera, she turns these everyday apertures into a way of capturing images and watching the world exist in our absence. “These images usually go unnoticed, blending into the ambient light, but even when we pay no attention, light is constantly creating images,” Nozomi Suzuki tells Blind . “I feel that these invisible images are like monologues whispered by light itself.” What does light say when we let it speak? It answers in its own vocabulary, a multitude of traces, stains, and silhouettes laid down on photosensitive paper. Unsuspected manifestations of the world, instantaneous and tangible, take shape from the point of view of objects, which watch us in return. To see… and to be seen.

The T3 Photo Festival Tokyo is on view in the Japanese capital city through October 26, 2026, in the Yaesu, Nihonbashi, Kyobashi, and Ginza districts. Free admission.

article_text:
SPOILERS: This post contains details about the Peacock series Friday the 13th

With the Friday the 13th prequel series Crystal Lake , longtime fans are treated to a backstory for the mother of all slashers.

Linda Cardellini , who plays Jason Voorhees’ grieving mother Pam in the Peacock series from Brad Caleb Kane, which is now available to stream, explained to Deadline that she used the maternal character’s grief as “fuel for her rage,” which ultimately pushes her to take murderous action months after her son Jason (Callum Vinson) drowns in the titular lake.

“It’s an interesting line that I walk as Pam because there’s part of her that doesn’t believe he’s totally gone, so there’s a real grief and a real longing that happens, but also hidden in there is a real hope that he might still be out there somewhere,” she explained. “So, that’s a really fun thing to play, because sometimes it can be total grief, and sometimes it can be in pain, and sometimes it can be grief hidden with a little bit of hope for who might be around the corner. And I think as that starts to pick up with her, that grief turns.”

Watch on Deadline

Linda Cardellini Admits She “Wanted” To Recreate Pamela Voorhees’ Haircut For ‘Crystal Lake’: “We Tried It For A Second”

Cardellini continued, “But I think the real grief is how people have treated him, because he’s such a sweet vulnerable kid when we first meet him, and she loves him so much. Watching the world treat him poorly is terrible for her, and the idea of that continues to just spiral out of control and it goes to the place that she fears the most, fuel for her rage. And I think that that rage is relatable. I think that it overtakes her though. I think finally releasing that rage overtakes her, and it feels a little too good to her, so there’s a switch that comes on after that.”

Set several years before the events of Friday the 13th (1980), the prequel series gives Pam her first taste for blood as a pair of mysterious men come poking around about her past. She uses a familiar weapon to get rid of them.

“The first one with the machete, I enjoy. That was big,” said Cardellini. “We shot that for a week, that whole sequence, so we really took time with it, which was nice.”

As she grieves the loss of her son, Pam takes a maternal interest in Jason’s friend Grace (Gwendolyn Sundstrom), whom she notices has a neglectful mother. While confronting Grace’s mom at the fast-food restaurant where she works, Pam takes the squabble a little too far.

“There is some anger that comes out when I have a mallet in the fast food restaurant,” recalled Cardellini. “And that seething anger, before that kill really happens, was I think somewhere, that something needed to come out of her. So, that was a fun one for me.”

Now streaming on Peacock, Crystal Lake stars Cardellini as Pam Voorhees, who struggles to grieve after her son Jason drowned the summer before. As two strangers begin digging into her mysterious past, Pam goes to murderous lengths to keep her secrets buried and find her son, whom she’s convinced is still alive after his body was never recovered.

article_text:
W hat on earth is happening at Button House? Kitty has tasered a police officer. Fanny is pulling down her capacious Victorian drawers to show off her bottom. Robin the caveman has fallen in love with a crusty eco activist (to be fair she looks quite a bit like him). If you’ve never watched the BBC’s haunted house comedy Ghosts – one of the finest family television shows in recent memory – none of the above will make the slightest bit of sense. Neither perhaps will this glorious new film, which picks up with the ghosts not long after the events of the final episode in 2023 .

Often when British sitcoms get a spin-off what happens is the gag-to-runtime ratio dips. But breaking out of the 30-minute episode structure seems to have freed up the writers to unleash new levels of giddiness with added spoonfuls of silliness. The jokes keep coming, and it’s every bit as warm and comforting as on TV.

It’s been a few months since Alison and Mike (Charlotte Ritchie and Kiell Smith-Bynoe) left Button House, selling the crumbling stately pile to a hotel chain. But work on the refurb has stalled, and the ghosts are pining after Alison, the only living person who can see them (long story). One of the joys of Ghosts is the competing main character energy of Button House’s deceased residents, played to perfection by an unassailable cast. There’s the sleazy Tory MP with no trousers, Julian Fawcett (Simon Farnaby), forever caught with his pants down. And scoutmaster Pat (Jim Howick) with an arrow through his neck. It feels mean to leave out the rest; each and every ghost could single-handedly power a 90-minute script. To say anything about the plot would ruin the fun. (I watched with a nine-year-old who hooted throughout.) It really is a delight.

"text": "我喜欢捕捉女儿在表达自我时双手的吉光片羽。她还年轻，但对这个世界的问题有着清晰透彻的理解。我常常想象她的双手拾起这个破碎世界的碎片并将其重塑，在纠正所有错误的过程中竭尽全力、不留遗憾。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "受这些想象的启发，我收集并打乱了现成的图像，加入女儿的双手来进行某种发掘，去寻找并重新排列破碎的事物，从而构建崭新的东西。这是一个充满希望的过程。这些图像是对她的双手以及它们在创造更美好世界方面将要完成的一切的颂歌。 —— 阿历克斯·弗朗戈斯", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-4.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 4", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的作品延伸了摄影媒介的边界。拼贴是如何成为你作品的核心焦点的？拼贴过程能让你表达什么是一张直拍照片所无法表达的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从我在大学上第一节暗房课起，我就有一种篡改图像的冲动，无论是划破底片还是在冲印后剪碎图像。部分原因是一种淘气和反叛规则的欲望；对于摄影师来说，没有什么比在冲印件或图像上划刻或剪裁更令人震惊的了。更重要的是，它为我提供了一种直接的方式来触及图像的潜意识含义，根据我的内在现实对其进行改造。随着时间推移，拼贴成为了我理解世界以及我在其中位置的主要方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-5.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 5", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《（重）排列》中的图像让人联想起20世纪20年代达达主义运动的蒙太奇艺术家。你在创作这组作品时受到了哪些影响？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我还是个青少年时，我发现了达达主义、超现实主义和俄国构成主义，我的世界瞬间被打开了。图像中多面向的现实深深触动了我。我有平面设计的背景，像汉娜·霍奇（Hannah Höch）和瓦尔瓦拉·斯捷潘诺娃（Varvara Stepanova）这样的艺术家打破了我陈旧的设计观念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "特别是在这个系列中，克劳德·卡洪（Claude Cahun）和马塞尔·摩尔（Marcel Moore）的摄影蒙太奇给予了我滋养。她们的摄影蒙太奇几乎是戏剧空间的延伸，并且这些图像所蕴含的自由似乎既包含了她们所生活的过去，也包含了未来。她们的图像是对自身关系的个人探索，却又容纳了如此丰富的内容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-6.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 6", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在这个系列中，你既使用了现成的照片，也使用了你自己的照片。使用你自己的照片对你来说重要吗？你如何决定何时融入其他素材？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个系列的契机非常简单，源于我拍摄女儿双手的冲动。她的双手既有着美丽娇嫩的质感，又带着坚定的力量。于是，尽管她感到有些困惑，我还是开始闯入她的生活去拍摄她的双手！正是在这段时间里，我在一家旧货店偶然看到了一本关于插花的旧书。我立刻萌生了一个想法：把她的双手加入书中的插花作品里，就好像她是这些美丽之作的缔造者。作品由此发展开来，并融入了其他现成的花卉意象以及真实的鲜花。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我确实喜欢在我的拼贴作品中融入我自己的照片。我记得帕蒂·史密斯（Patti Smith）在她的一本书《只是孩子》（Just Kids）中写到过，罗伯特·梅普尔索普（Robert Mapplethorpe）认为当拼贴画融入他自己的照片时会更加诚实。这个想法深深印在了我的脑海里。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-8.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 8", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你是从一个具体的构思和愿景开始创作，还是作品完全在实验和直觉中自然流淌出来？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的创作过程非常直觉化。通常，我先收集那些让我产生情感共鸣的影像，所以对这个项目来说，它是从我女儿手部的照片以及那本插花书中的图片开始的。等积累了一大堆图片后，我便凭直觉开始剪裁和拼接——把图像组合在一起，有时用胶带，有时加入新剪下的鲜花。这是我创作中最喜欢的部分，并且非常具有游戏感。很多时候，这些拼贴感觉像是失败了，但有时我会看到某种画面开始显现。接着，摄影的过程就开始了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-9.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 9", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些作品既好玩又美丽，同时由于画面中的手臂是无躯干的，它们又有一种引人注目的震撼感。这种二元性是有意为之的吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些作品很大程度上源于我们所处的黑暗时代。创作它们，有点像是在用我对女儿及其一代人能够建设更美好世界的信念来对抗这种黑暗。我们的许多体制都已崩解，无论好坏，而看着她这一代人以如此富有同情心和正义感的方式作出回应，正是这黑暗中的光芒。所以是的，我认为这种二元性是有意为之的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-10.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no.10", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你最近有一组作品《Ghosts of Displacement》，讲述了你家族作为难民和美国移民的历史，而现在这个系列则聚焦于你的女儿。你能谈谈家庭在你的作品中所代表的重要性，以及跨越世代进行影像创作对你意味着什么吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的作品一直都带有极强的个人色彩。《Ghosts of Displacement》探讨的是我作为移民子女和孙辈的自身身份。在花费了大量时间创作一个关于家族史的项目之后，我想转向家族的未来是一个顺理成章的冲动——尽管我在当时并没有意识到自己正在这样做。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-12.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 12", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "诗人玛丽·奥利弗（Mary Oliver）写道：“关注是全身心投入的开始。”创作这些影像有没有改变你和女儿之间的关系？她对这组作品有什么看法？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这组作品很大程度上关乎我对女儿感到的爱与骄傲，而创作过程本身就是一种沉思这些感受的方式。因此，它只会加深我对她的爱与理解。她是个内向的人，成为这些照片的主角让她觉得有点不好意思。作为同样内向的人，我完全理解这一点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-13.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 13", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个系列有一种元叙事的质感，因为你是用自己的双手在创作一个关于“手”的系列。这些影像在某种程度上是否也代表了你自身想要让世界变得更好的愿望？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我从来没这么想过！由于世间万物皆由双手衍生，手一直是我最喜欢的主题。我似乎只有通过双手去操纵和剪裁影像才能进行创作，并且在创造出的影像中构建出我想要映射的世界。所以，尽管我之前没有意识到，但我想你是对的！", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-14.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 14", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你接下来还有什么其他的创作计划？关于你的艺术实践，还有什么你想让我们知道的吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我目前正在做一个暗室系列，涉及在暗室打印之前对找到的底片进行切割和拼凑。这与我的芭蕾舞背景以及它对我产生的影响有关。因此，我仍在顺从自己的冲动，将图像的破坏作为一种创作形式。你可以在Perspective Gallery的网站上看到更多本次展览中的作品。你可以通过我的网站alexafrangos.com与我联系，或在Instagram上关注我@alexafrangos。", "links": [{"text": "Perspective Gallery", "url": "https://perspectivegallery.org/october-2026"}, {"text": "alexafrangos.com", "url": "https://alexafrangos.com/home.html"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "苏珊·艾萨克森（Susan Isaacson）是一位摄影艺术家，致力于探索时间、记忆以及生活转折期情感地形的主题。她被自然景观所吸引，以此作为连接和表达其内心世界的方式。她的作品受到正念研究和犹太教的影响，犹太教强调时间的圣洁性。", "links": [{"text": "Susan Isaacson", "url": "https://www.susanisaacsonphotography.com/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在一家《财富》100强企业经历了20年的战略市场营销职业生涯后，艾萨克森在伊利诺伊州芝加哥和加利福尼亚州拉古纳海滩建立了一个专注的摄影工作室。她的作品曾在美国及国际上的多个群展中展出。艾萨克森由伊利诺伊州埃文斯顿的Alta Vista Arts和Perspective Gallery代理，在那里她举办了4次个展并联合策展了3次会员展。艾萨克森的系列作品《We Share The Same Breath》入选2023年Critical Mass前200名决赛入围者，其项目《At Silver Lake》于2024年再次入围。艾萨克森的作品曾被《Black + White Photography》（英国）、《SHOTS Magazine》、《Photo Trouvee Magazine》、《LENSCRATCH》、《NewCity Art》和《All About A Photo》等刊物报道。她的作品被美国境内的私人收藏机构所收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Instagram: @sbisaacson", "links": [{"text": "@sbisaacson", "url": "https://instagram.com/sbisaacson"}], I’m continually intrigued by her thought-provoking and evocative work. Her practice early on stretched beyond conventional photography into the realm of photo-collage, where she conjures surrealistic imagery by hand. She has tackled topics as widespread and meaningful as honoring the legacy of her immigrant and refugee family history in Ghosts Of Displacement to eulogizing the dying art of celluloid cinema in Zoetrope .", "links": [{"text": "Alexa Frangos", "url": "https://alexafrangos.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frangos now turns her attention to the workings of her daughter’s hands in a hopeful and poetic collection entitled (Re)arranging . Playful and performative, the work looks both back to Surrealist photography of the 1920s and 1930s and forward to the potential of today’s younger generations to create a more beautiful world. (Re)arranging is currently on exhibition at Perspective Gallery in Evanston, IL through November 1st. Frangos will give an on-line Artist talk Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, 7 p.m. CT . You can follow this link to register for the talk at Perspective Gallery.", "links": [{"text": "Perspective Gallery", "url": "https://perspectivegallery.org/october-2026"}, {"text": "Artist talk Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, 7 p.m. CT", "url": "https://us02web.zoom.us/meeting/register/4z6gmkklRO2ou2bE31pZgQ#/registration"}, {"text": "link", "url": "https://perspectivegallery.org/october-2026"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An interview with the artist follows."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-2.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 2"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alexa Frangos (b. 1973) is a photo-based artist from Chicago, Illinois. Utilizing cut paper, photographic ephemera and found objects, Frangos creates constructed realities that seek to reflect on psychological states and identity. She is especially drawn to the collage process as a source of play, performance, and transformation. Frangos studied Visual Communications and Photography at Washington University in St. Louis before receiving her M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, where her multimedia work evolved into a photographic practice. She then attended law school and practiced law for many years before returning to art full-time. She has been showing work nationally and internationally since 2012. In 2021 she won a Julia Margaret Cameron award for her series Ghosts of Displacement. In 2024 she was one of Photolucida’s Top 200. Her work has been featured in F-Stop Magazine, Contemporary Collage Magazine, Photo Trouvée Magazine, The Hand Magazine, Newcity Art and Lenscratch.", "links": [{"text": "Alexa Frangos", "url": "https://alexafrangos.com/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Instagram: @alexafrangos"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 3"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Every human being is an artist, a freedom being, called to participate in transforming and reshaping the conditions, thinking and structures that shape and inform our lives.” ― Joseph Beuys"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I love to catch a glimpse of my daughter’s hands while she is expressing herself. She is still young, but has a crystal clear grasp of what is wrong with the world. I often imagine her hands picking up the pieces of this shattered world and remaking it, leaving nothing undone in her efforts to right all the wrongs."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Inspired by these imaginings, I’ve gathered and disrupted found images, adding my daughter’s hands to perform a sort of excavation, finding and rearranging what is broken and building something new. It is a hopeful process. These images live as an ode to her hands, and all that they will accomplish in creating a better world. – Alexa Frangos"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-4.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 4"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Your work stretches the boundaries of the photographic medium. How did collage become a central focus in your work? What is it that the collage process allows you to express that you couldn’t with a straight photograph?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "From the time I took my first darkroom class in college I’ve had the impulse to alter my images, whether it was scratching into the negatives or cutting up the images after printing. Partly it was a desire to be naughty and to go against the rules; there is nothing more shocking to photographers than scratching or cutting into a print or image. More importantly, it afforded me a direct way to get to the subconscious meaning of an image, to alter it according to my inner reality. Over time, collage became my primary way of making sense of the world and my place in it."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-5.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 5"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The images in (Re)arranging are reminiscent of photomontage artists of the Dada movement in the 1920’s. What were your influences in making this work?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When I was a teen, I discovered Dada, Surrealism and Russian Constructivism and my world cracked open. The multifaceted reality of the imagery deeply resonated with me. I come from a background in graphic design, and artists like Hannah Höch and Varvara Stepanova broke apart my staid ideas of design."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Especially for this series, I was nourished by the photomontages of Claude Cahun and Marcel Moore. The way their photomontages were almost an extension of a theatrical space, and the way the freedom of these images seemed to contain both the past they were living in and the future. Their images were a personal exploration of their own relationship but contained so much more."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-6.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 6"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In this collection you work with both found photographs and your own. Is it important to you to use your own photographs? How do you decide when to incorporate other source materials?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The way this series started was the simple impulse I had to photograph my daughter’s hands. Her hands are beautifully delicate, and yet so strong with purpose. So, I started interrupting her life to photograph her hands, much to her bemusement! It was during this period that I came upon an old book on flower arranging at a thrift store. I was immediately struck with the idea of adding her hands to the floral arrangements in the book, as if she was the author of their beauty. The work grew from there to include other found floral imagery and real flowers too."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I do like to include my own photographs in my collage work. I remember something Patti Smith wrote about in her book Just Kids , how Robert Mapplethorpe felt his collages were more honest when they incorporated his own photographs. That idea has stuck with me."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-8.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 8"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Do you start out with a vision in mind for a specific composition or do your pieces arise organically from experimentation and intuition?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My process is very intuitive. Typically, I start by collecting images that feel connected to me, so for this project it started with the photographs of my daughter’s hands and images from the book on flower arranging. This is my favorite part of the process, and it is very playful. Often the constructions felt like failures, but sometimes I saw an image emerging. Then the photographing begins."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-9.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 9"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "These images are playful and beautiful, and at the same time they are arresting because the arms in the frame are disembodied. So many of our systems have exploded, for better and for worse, and watching her generation respond with such compassion and righteousness is the light in this darkness. So yes, I think the duality is intentional."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://lenscratch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Frangos_Rearranging-no.-10.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Lenscratch"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no.10"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You have a recent body of work, Ghosts of Displacement , which speaks to your family’s history as refugees and immigrants to the United States and now in this series you are focused on your daughter. Could you speak to the importance of family represented in your work and what making images that span generations means to you?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My work has always been deeply personal.
