article_text:
Alexa Frangos: (Re)arranging

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 1

“She is still young, but has a crystal clear grasp of what is wrong with the world,” Frangos writes. “I often imagine her hands picking up the pieces of this shattered world and remaking it, leaving nothing undone in her efforts to right all the wrongs.”

I’ve had the pleasure of knowing Alexa Frangos for over ten years after meeting her in a critique class at a local Chicago art center. I’m continually intrigued by her thought-provoking and evocative work. Her practice early on stretched beyond conventional photography into the realm of photo-collage, where she conjures surrealistic imagery by hand. She has tackled topics as widespread and meaningful as honoring the legacy of her immigrant and refugee family history in Ghosts Of Displacement to eulogizing the dying art of celluloid cinema in Zoetrope .

Frangos now turns her attention to the workings of her daughter’s hands in a hopeful and poetic collection entitled (Re)arranging . Playful and performative, the work looks both back to Surrealist photography of the 1920s and 1930s and forward to the potential of today’s younger generations to create a more beautiful world. (Re)arranging is currently on exhibition at Perspective Gallery in Evanston, IL through November 1st. Frangos will give an on-line Artist talk Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, 7 p.m. CT . You can follow this link to register for the talk at Perspective Gallery.

An interview with the artist follows.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 2

Alexa Frangos (b. 1973) is a photo-based artist from Chicago, Illinois. Utilizing cut paper, photographic ephemera and found objects, Frangos creates constructed realities that seek to reflect on psychological states and identity. She is especially drawn to the collage process as a source of play, performance, and transformation. Frangos studied Visual Communications and Photography at Washington University in St. Louis before receiving her M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago, where her multimedia work evolved into a photographic practice. She then attended law school and practiced law for many years before returning to art full-time. She has been showing work nationally and internationally since 2012. In 2021 she won a Julia Margaret Cameron award for her series Ghosts of Displacement. In 2024 she was one of Photolucida’s Top 200. Her work has been featured in F-Stop Magazine, Contemporary Collage Magazine, Photo Trouvée Magazine, The Hand Magazine, Newcity Art and Lenscratch.

Instagram: @alexafrangos

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 3

“Every human being is an artist, a freedom being, called to participate in transforming and reshaping the conditions, thinking and structures that shape and inform our lives.” ― Joseph Beuys

I love to catch a glimpse of my daughter’s hands while she is expressing herself. She is still young, but has a crystal clear grasp of what is wrong with the world. I often imagine her hands picking up the pieces of this shattered world and remaking it, leaving nothing undone in her efforts to right all the wrongs.

Inspired by these imaginings, I’ve gathered and disrupted found images, adding my daughter’s hands to perform a sort of excavation, finding and rearranging what is broken and building something new. It is a hopeful process. These images live as an ode to her hands, and all that they will accomplish in creating a better world. – Alexa Frangos

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 4

Your work stretches the boundaries of the photographic medium. How did collage become a central focus in your work? What is it that the collage process allows you to express that you couldn’t with a straight photograph?

From the time I took my first darkroom class in college I’ve had the impulse to alter my images, whether it was scratching into the negatives or cutting up the images after printing. Partly it was a desire to be naughty and to go against the rules; there is nothing more shocking to photographers than scratching or cutting into a print or image. More importantly, it afforded me a direct way to get to the subconscious meaning of an image, to alter it according to my inner reality. Over time, collage became my primary way of making sense of the world and my place in it.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 5

The images in (Re)arranging are reminiscent of photomontage artists of the Dada movement in the 1920’s. What were your influences in making this work?

When I was a teen, I discovered Dada, Surrealism and Russian Constructivism and my world cracked open. The multifaceted reality of the imagery deeply resonated with me. I come from a background in graphic design, and artists like Hannah Höch and Varvara Stepanova broke apart my staid ideas of design.

Especially for this series, I was nourished by the photomontages of Claude Cahun and Marcel Moore. The way their photomontages were almost an extension of a theatrical space, and the way the freedom of these images seemed to contain both the past they were living in and the future. Their images were a personal exploration of their own relationship but contained so much more.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 6

In this collection you work with both found photographs and your own. Is it important to you to use your own photographs? How do you decide when to incorporate other source materials?

The way this series started was the simple impulse I had to photograph my daughter’s hands. Her hands are beautifully delicate, and yet so strong with purpose. So, I started interrupting her life to photograph her hands, much to her bemusement! It was during this period that I came upon an old book on flower arranging at a thrift store. I was immediately struck with the idea of adding her hands to the floral arrangements in the book, as if she was the author of their beauty. The work grew from there to include other found floral imagery and real flowers too.

I do like to include my own photographs in my collage work. I remember something Patti Smith wrote about in her book Just Kids , how Robert Mapplethorpe felt his collages were more honest when they incorporated his own photographs. That idea has stuck with me.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 8

Do you start out with a vision in mind for a specific composition or do your pieces arise organically from experimentation and intuition?

My process is very intuitive. Typically, I start by collecting images that feel connected to me, so for this project it started with the photographs of my daughter’s hands and images from the book on flower arranging. After I have a large pile of images, I start cutting and assembling intuitively – piecing the images together, sometimes with tape, sometimes adding freshly cut flowers. This is my favorite part of the process, and it is very playful. Often the constructions felt like failures, but sometimes I saw an image emerging. Then the photographing begins.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 9

These images are playful and beautiful, and at the same time they are arresting because the arms in the frame are disembodied. Was this duality intentional?

So much about these images arose from the dark times we are living in. Making them was a bit like combating this darkness with the faith I have in my daughter and her generation to build a better world. So many of our systems have exploded, for better and for worse, and watching her generation respond with such compassion and righteousness is the light in this darkness. So yes, I think the duality is intentional.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no.10

You have a recent body of work, Ghosts of Displacement , which speaks to your family’s history as refugees and immigrants to the United States and now in this series you are focused on your daughter. Could you speak to the importance of family represented in your work and what making images that span generations means to you?

My work has always been deeply personal. Ghosts of Displacement was about exploring my own identity as the child and grandchild of immigrants. After spending so much time on a project about my family history, I suppose it was a natural impulse to pivot to the future of my family. Although I didn’t realize that was what I was doing at the time.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 12

Poet Mary Oliver wrote, “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” Has making these images changed anything in the relationship between you and your daughter? What does she think about the work?

This work is so much about the love and pride I feel toward my daughter and working on it has been a way to meditate on these feelings. So, it has only strengthened my love and understanding of her. She is an introvert and being the subject of these photographs is a bit embarrassing to her. As an introvert myself I understand.

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 13

This series has a meta feel, in that you are using your hands to make a series about hands. Do these images in some way represent your own desire to better the world?

I never thought of that! Hands have always been a favorite subject of mine because of everything that springs from them. The only way I can seem to make work is by manipulating and cutting images with my hands, and within the images I create the world I want to reflect. So even though it didn’t occur to me, I think you are right!

©Alexa Frangos, (Re)arranging no. 14

What other projects are on your horizon? Is there anything else you would like us to know about your practice?

I am currently working on a darkroom series that involves cutting and piecing together found negatives before printing them in the darkroom. It is about my background in ballet and the impact it had on me. So, I am still following my impulse to use image destruction as a form of creation. You can see more of the work included in this exhibition on the Perspective Gallery website. You can contact me on my website alexafrangos.com or find me on instagram @alexafrangos.

Susan Isaacson is a photographic artist exploring themes of time, memory, and the emotional topography of life transitions. She is drawn to the natural landscape as a means to connect with and represent her inner world. Her work is influenced by studies of mindfulness and Judaism, with its emphasis on the sanctification of time.

Following a twenty-year career in strategic marketing at a Fortune 100 company, Isaacson established a dedicated photography practice in Chicago, Illinois and Laguna Beach, California. Her work has been included in group exhibitions across the U.S. and internationally. Isaacson is represented by Alta Vista Arts and Perspective Gallery in Evanston IL, where she has mounted four solo exhibitions and co-curated three member exhibitions. Isaacson was recognized as a Critical Mass Top 200 Finalist in 2023 for her series, We Share The Same Breath and again in 2024 for her project, At Silver Lake. Isaacson’s work has been featured in Black + White Photography (UK), SHOTS Magazine, Photo Trouvee Magazine, LENSCRATCH, NewCity Art and All About A Photo. Her work is held in private collections within the United States.

Instagram: @sbisaacson

article_text:
Rise and Shine World Sales has secured international rights to Elwira Niewiera’s documentary “Women and War,” which follows four Ukrainian women, all survivors of war crimes, undergoing trauma therapy in the Ukrainian mountains. The film is set to world premiere in the Main Competition at the International Documentary Festival Amsterdam, taking place Nov. 12-22.

“Women and War” follows the personal journeys of Olena, Yuliia, Iryna and Lena, who survived the nightmares of the ongoing Russian war against Ukraine. Over the course of one year, the film follows the women through long-term therapy in the remote Ukrainian mountains, where they slowly begin to heal under the care of therapists and psychologists.

Related Stories

Having survived captivity, torture, sexual violence, months hiding in dark basements and the loss of loved ones, each woman follows her own path toward recovery. The therapy provides them a safe space to confront the lasting effects of their traumatic experiences and gradually regain emotional and physical balance. Through their stories, the film offers a female-focused perspective on resilience, inner strength and the struggle to reclaim their lives.

Niewiera says, “For years, I’ve been working alongside women in Ukraine who have survived war crimes, and one thing has become very clear: for them, the war does not end when the weapons fall silent. It remains present in their thoughts, in their bodies, and in their daily routines. Violence against women in conflict is still frequently ignored, despite the fact that rape and torture are deliberately used as tools to break women and destabilize entire communities.”

She added, “As a filmmaker and as a woman, I felt a responsibility to give these women a space where their voices could be heard. I didn’t want to define them only through their trauma. I wanted to show their courage, their strength and the small steps they take toward healing.

“There are very painful moments, but there is also warmth, empathy. For me, it was important to show that these women are much more than their traumatic experiences. I want this film to give these women back their dignity and show the world how incredibly strong and determined they are to reclaim their lives. For me, making this film was also a way of taking action. I wanted to raise awareness of the long-term consequences of war and the urgent need to support survivors worldwide.”

Anja Dziersk of Rise and Shine said, “It is well known that violence against women has been used as a weapon of war for centuries. But it is hard to think of a film that places the horrors of imprisonment and torture in a context that draws the viewer in on such an emotional level. Elwira Niewiera shines a light on the fact that war is not waged only on the battlefield. We admire the courage and strength of these women, who open up in conversation and confront their trauma as part of the healing process. This is a film about life. About how you can go on after the unimaginable has happened to you.”

“Women and War” is produced by Hans Robert Eisenhauer for Germany’s Ventana Film, Maciej Kubicki for Poland-based Telemark and Natalia Krasilnikova for Art Dialogue in Ukraine. It is co-produced with ZDF and TVP, in cooperation with ARTE.

Niewiera’s previous works, “The Hamlet Syndrome” (2022), “The Prince and the Dybbuk” (2017) and “The Domino Effect” (2014), have screened at major festivals including Venice Film Festival, Locarno Film Festival, IDFA , Hot Docs, DOK Leipzig and Krakow Film Festival.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Narges Rashidi , who recently won the BAFTA for Leading Actress for her portrayal of Nazanin Zaghari Ratcliffe in BBC’s Prisoner 951 , has signed with TFC Management .

The series, directed by Phillipa Lowthorpe and also starring Joseph Fiennes, told the true story of Zaghari Ratfcliffe’s wrongful seven-year imprisonment in Iran and her husband’s subsequent fight for her release. In addition to the BAFTA, Narges also received two Royal Television Society Awards along with several other award nominations for her portrayal of Nazanin.

Narges is perhaps best known in the U.S. and the UK for her role as fearless mobster Lale in Gangs of London for Sky/AMC, which is heading into its fourth and final season in 2027. Narges also performs the majority of her own stunts across the series.

Lucius Cary Joins TFC Management

Her breakthrough role was leading Babak Anvari’s 2016 acclaimed and award-winning Persian-language film Under the Shadow , which premiered at the Sundance Film Festival. For her performance, Narges received a nomination for Best Actress at the BIFAs, a well as the Breakthrough Actress award at the New York International Film Festival.

Narges’ other credits include Netflix feature Havoc opposite Tom Hardy and indie feature Last Swim , which won at Berlinale 2025. Narges has a long list of German credits including series The Allegation , which won the Dior Grand Prize at Canneseries in 2021.

Founded in 2020 by David Stone and Ben Jacobson, TFC Management reps on-camera talents such as Dakota and Elle Fanning, Shira Haas, Lashana Lynch, JD Pardo, Dan Ings and Josh Hutcherson, as well as such creators, filmmakers, novelists and producers as Warren Littlefield, Brian Yorkey, Megan Park, Adam Reed, Akiva Goldsman, Courtney Lilly, Josh & Jonas Pate and Rebecca Serle.

TFC’s sister company, TFC Productions, most recently produced the Apple series Margo’s Got Money Troubles , created by David E. Kelley and starring Elle Fanning, which recently received eight Emmy nominations , including Outstanding Comedy Series.

Rashidi will continue to be repped by The Artists Partnership in all areas.

article_text:
Book Review

The Trafficker Who Furnished the Museums of LA

A team of researchers excavates the story of Earl Stendahl, a mid-century gallerist who shamelessly stole ancient Mesoamerican objects and marketed them to the institutional art world.

In a 1940 photograph by Man Ray, Academy Award-winning actor Teresa Wright poses misty-eyed alongside an ancient Chacmool sculpture. The reclining figure, with its head contorted toward viewers, offered a refreshed vision of modernity to both Hollywood stars and a growing clientele of collectors and museums interested in pre-colonial art from ancient Mesoamerica. In 1947, for instance, the Minneapolis Institute of Art purchased a “King Chak Mool” for $10,000. That sculpture toured Europe as part of an exhibition from 1958 to 1960 and quickly became a cornerstone of the museum’s collection. Just a decade later, one specialist made a dreaded discovery: The sculpture was a forgery.

This story, and that of the gallerist at its center, is chronicled in Artifacts to Art: Collecting Ancient America in Midcentury L.A. (2026) by Andrew D. Turner, Mary E. Miller, and Khristaan D. Villela. The book elaborates on the various conditions that shifted the classification of “pre-Hispanic” artifacts from anthropological items of study to art objects that could be collected by museums and patrons alike. It also helped answer a question I’ve always had about Los Angeles museums as a curator myself: Why is so much cultural heritage of ancient Central and South America preserved in our city’s collections?

As Artifacts to Art discusses, the Stendahl Art Galleries were a key driver in the illegal looting, smuggling, and sale of these objects to its Los Angeles clientele. The Galleries’ archive is now housed at the Getty Research Institute (which published this book), allowing for a deep investigation into the shady dealings of an art dealer who had little regard for the cultural histories he exploited. Turner, Miller, and Villela present five years of groundbreaking research into that archive here. Over its non-chronological chapters, the book describes the various forces that collided to create a market for these objects, including revered international museums, Hollywood actors, and looters across Mexico.

Exhibitionist: Earl Stendahl, Art Dealer as Impresario (2011)

Earl Stendahl began his career as an art dealer by selling paintings on the walls of his restaurant in downtown Los Angeles after relocating from Wisconsin in 1911. By 1921, he was involved in the city’s early development projects and opened the Stendahl Art Galleries at the historic Ambassador Hotel on Wilshire Boulevard, where celebrities and political elite window-shopped the art on offer. In just a few years, Stendahl fostered relationships with dealers, collectors, and artists, which opened pathways for him to exhibit works by Diego Rivera and David Alfaro Siqueiros and led him to stage the only Los Angeles presentation of Pablo Picasso’s “Guernica” (1937) for eleven days in 1939. This display was controversial in the lead-up to World War II, and it also signaled Stendahl’s propensity for risk-taking, especially if it lined his pockets.

As the authors explain, one of the key relationships Stendahl established at the Ambassador Hotel was with the collectors Walter and Louise Arensberg. The couple migrated from New York to Los Angeles and were among the biggest collectors of objects from ancient America, despite never setting foot in Mexico. They were quick to juxtapose Indigenous objects with European avant-garde art in their home; some of these displays were captured in a 1945 Vogue article. This comparison suggested that modernity’s roots were aesthetically connected to an ancient past, while also emphasizing the time between the objects and decentering Europe as the movement’s birthplace. As the Vogue article suggests, it also emphasized the role that Western collectors played in reclassifying “ancient artifacts” as “art.”

Wealthy patrons were just one part of Stendahl’s equation. In 1935, he received a visit from Guillermo Echániz, a Mexican collector, antiquarian, and librarian. The two immediately colluded to steal antiquities from Mexico’s ancient cultural sites, including Jaina, a Maya burial island. Echániz worked with huaqueros , or looters, to extract these objects and smuggle them into the United States. Often, they were altered by Stendahl or fabricated by local artisans in Mexico, a history of which is well documented in Artifacts to Art . The authors articulate the violence of such acts, writing that “it is painful to imagine the looter or dealer defacing, quite literally, the ancient object.” By 1941, Stendahl had amassed an inventory of artifacts, as he notes in a letter to an archaeologist: “You will marvel at the great number of good things I have been able to gather in the past six years.”

article_text:
Amazon MGM Studios Japan is doubling its investment to bring its content up to global standards, studio head Buddy Marini said Wednesday at a Tokyo International Film Festival TIFFCOM market session on unlocking the global potential of Japanese IP.

The session, organized by the Motion Picture Association (MPA) and UniJapan, also featured Credeus CEO Matsuhashi Shinzo and “One Piece” Netflix series executive producer Steven Maeda, with entertainment sociologist and consultant Nakayama Atsuo serving as moderator.

Related Stories

Disney Names Carol Choi Asia Pacific President as Luke Kang Retires

Marini, who was appointed head of the Japan studio in March, is in charge of its homegrown film, series and anime productions. He previously served as managing director of Warner Bros. Discovery Japan and CEO of Hulu Japan, and founded Mangamo.

He began by explaining how his platform “manages everything – from the initial idea stage through planning, development, strategy, investment, and all the way to the final product.”

The basic strategy for both Japan and the Amazon studio as a whole, he added, is to “expand into the global market.” “There are all kinds of viewers, so the goal is to reach all of them,” he said. “So we’re handling all kinds of content, regardless of genre.”

That is also true of other platforms, but Marini believes that Amazon is unique in offering various benefits to its Prime members – movies being among them. “Our primary objective has always been to delight the audience in that specific country or region,” he said. “But in doing that we’ve started to make our mark in various places around the world. Since our service is global, our audience isn’t really concerned with which country the content is from. They just think, ‘If it’s interesting, it’s interesting.’ So, we’re doubling our investment to ensure that quality meets global standards.”

Among upcoming projects on his studio’s slate are “The Apothecary Diaries,” a live-action adaptation of a bestselling historical mystery franchise, and “Bless,” a live-action adaptation of a hit manga about an aspiring makeup artist.

Among past Japanese-language hits on Amazon Prime is “The Silent Service,” a live-action series about a rogue Japanese submarine captain who hijacks a U.S. sub, based on a long-running manga that also generated a hit anime series. “We’ve achieved some amazing results with the series,” commented Marini, “but it’s difficult to maintain that level of quality.”

“When it comes to elevating our content to IPs that can resonate globally, I truly believe that the reverse-engineering process is the most important factor,” Marini said. “So, within our team, the creative staff works closely with the screenwriters to develop the scripts and ensure that from a global perspective, we’re crafting a story that’s truly compelling.”

Also on the panel was Matsuhashi, whose credits as producer include last year’s smash “Kokuho,” which set an all-time box office record for Japanese live-action films, as well as the “Kingdom” period action series, the “Gintama” action comedy series, “Blue Lock” and “Golden Kamuy.” He joined Wowow in 1994, made his producing debut with “Battle Royale,” went independent in 2005 and started his present company, Credeus, about eight years ago. “I realized I wouldn’t be able to make the kind of work I envisioned unless I did that, so that’s the choice I made,” he said.

As a producer Matsuhashi has developed what he calls the “right production ratio.” “First and foremost, the story has to be interesting,” he said. “Then it needs to be turned into an interesting script. Then you bring in an excellent director and crew and assemble a great cast. I believe that only when these elements come together does a work come as close as possible to success.”

The proof that this “ratio” is indeed right is Matsuhashi’s sterling track record – the films he has produced passed JPY100 billion ($633 million) in cumulative box office this year.

His breakthrough was the “Kingdom” historical action/drama series, which is set in China’s Warring States period and is based on a popular manga. Launched in 2019, it now totals five feature entries.

The start, Matsuhashi said, came when Sanford Panitch, who was then in charge of international production for Sony Pictures, approached him about making local films for Japan. “I asked him if he wanted to fill a production quota with three films or revolutionize Japanese movies,” Matsuhashi recalled. When Panitch opted for the latter, Matsuhashi brought him a concept for three “Kingdom” films. “I told him that the three-film package was a single business venture, so I wanted him to invest in it. I doubt there are many projects created with this kind of specific plan in mind.”

Panitch signed on and the first three films each earned more than JPY5 billion ($31.7 million) – making them major hits at the Japanese box office. The moral: A bold vision, made with the right elements, can yield big returns.

Starting more than two decades ago, Matsuhashi has also negotiated a success fee for all of his projects. “It was something that hadn’t really been mainstream in Japan,” he said. “I’ve continued using this model for a long time – where the producer, the person actually creating the work, receives a success fee if it becomes a hit – and it’s gradually become established.”

Rounding out the panel was Maeda, executive producer of the Netflix live-action series “One Piece,” which topped the charts in 46 countries in its opening week in 2023 and racked up more than 140 million viewing hours over those first seven days. He also worked on “Lost,” “The X-Files” and “Lie to Me,” and is now adapting “Monstress,” the Eisner-winning graphic novel, for Amazon Prime Video alongside his partner Tiff Greshler and Hivemind Entertainment.

When he was approached by Tomorrow Studios about making a live-action version of “One Piece,” Maeda said he knew nothing about the manga, but “read the first hundred chapters… and I just loved it.” But he also wondered how they could make the series “since it was going to be so expensive.”

When Netflix became involved, Maeda remembered, “they wanted us to make it as cheaply as possible.” But he knew that fans would not be happy with a cut-rate “One Piece.” “They didn’t want us to make a bad version of one of their favorite anime or manga,” he said, “so we had to go in there and really convince (Netflix) that by making a show fans would appreciate, they also would attract a new audience.”

“That’s the battle of a lot of global IP,” he added. “You’re going to have people who love the show, and they want a faithful adaptation of that show. You’re going to have people who have never heard of the show, and you still need to bring those people in as well.”

“And if you succeed, you can have an international success,” Maeda said. “And if you fail, everyone hates you.”

article_text:
In 2024, AMC Theatres went viral after moviegoers discovered the sandworm-inspired popcorn bucket for “Dune: Part Two” was… suggestive, to say the least. The iconic vessel was the subject of countless memes and later immortalized on “Saturday Night Live” in a sketch about a teenager with other plans for the souvenir container.

Now the cinema chain is unveiling two new destined-to-break-the-internet designs for the upcoming “Dune: Part Three.” There’s a “Sandworm Thumper” with a “working Thumper design” (that’s the device used by the Freman to pound the desert sand and attract giant sandworms) and a “Double Sandworm” collectable featuring two Shai-Hulud, “making it easier to share popcorn,” according to AMC’s press release. Prices will be announced at a later date. (Canisters for “Dune: Part Two” were $24.99 plus tax but sold for much more on secondary markets like eBay.)

'KPop Demon Hunters,' 'Squid Game' Stars Fete Netflix's Korea Decade as Ted Sarandos Teases 'Tantara,' 'All of Us Are Dead' Season 2

AMC’s “Dune: Part Three” collection also has a Atreides-Fremen light-up cup, a spacing guild navigator cup, mystery keychains and sandworm plush. These items will be available exclusively at AMC locations as well as Odeon Cinemas throughout Europe.

“The AMC Sandworm popcorn bucket for ‘Dune: Part Two’ became a viral phenomenon, and we knew that ‘Dune’ fans would have high expectations for what came next,” said Hank Green, AMC’s senior VP of food and beverage. “From the moment we started planning the ‘Dune: Part Three’ collectibles, our goal was to exceed those fan expectations. The Sandworm Thumper and Double Sandworm collectibles take the experience to the next level with designs straight from the movie.”

Directed by Denis Villenueve and based on Frank Herbert’s novel, “ Dune 3 ” concludes the sci-fi trilogy as Timothée Chalamet’s messianic Paul Atreides is forced to contend with the fallout from his ascent to the throne. Zendaya, Robert Pattinson, Florence Pugh, Anya Taylor-Joy, Jason Momoa, Javier Bardem, Josh Brolin and Rebecca Ferguson round out the starry cast. “Dune: Part Three” opens in theaters on Dec. 18, the same day as “Avengers: Doomsday.” Disney Marvel’s epic is expected to ignite the box office, but will Earth’s Mightiest Heroes have a popcorn bucket that breaks the internet?

Me’展览分为四个篇章，以前所未有的规模在巴黎展出了皮诺收藏的摄影原作。”随着庆祝摄影诞生二百周年的活动日益增多，商业交易所将一直展出至2027年1月18日，展品是从收藏者拥有的8,000件藏品中遴选出的700多幅影像。他补充道：“这是一个以双重视角切入参观的机会：‘理解今天影像所面临的关键问题，同时也理解皮诺的收藏格局。’”展览追溯了从摄影发明到当今的历史，交替呈现群展和个展，完美契合了建筑的宏伟气势，旨在探讨照片在“影像泛滥的世界中质问我们的能力，同时向一门艺术及其与我们对话的能力致敬。”", article_text:
“Divided into four chapters, the ‘Remember Me’ exhibition makes it possible to show the prints of the Pinault Collection on a scale unprecedented in Paris,” says curator Matthieu Humery by way of introduction. As events marking the bicentenary of photography multiply, the Bourse de Commerce is showing, until January 18, 2027, more than 700 images from the 8,000 held by the collector. It is an opportunity to approach the visit with a double perspective: “understanding what is at stake in the image today, but also understanding the Pinault holdings,” he adds. Tracing the history of photography from its invention to the present day, the exhibition alternates group hangs and solo shows, sitting perfectly within the grandeur of the building, to question the capacity of photographs to “challenge us in a world where they proliferate, while paying tribute to an art and its ability to speak to us.”

At the very center of the museum, The History of Tears , a work by Barbara Kruger conceived specifically for the architecture of the rotunda, opens the show. Monumental, the installation sets words (those of George Orwell, Roland Barthes and Aimé Césaire) against powerful emotions. Pasted across the walls, the sentences collide with videos in a strange kind of dialogue where domination, anger and joy blend depending on the reading one chooses. “The three literary quotations make it possible to understand the logic behind the conception of the space. There is the political dimension, the romantic dimension, and the desire to resolve conflict,” explains Matthieu Humery.

An avalanche of images

Gallery 2 then plunges us into the world of Irving Penn. Here, 450 photographs dating from the 1940s to the 2000s line the upper reaches of the white walls, winding to the very limits of our vision. The effect is dizzying. “The idea here is to show the artist’s work in its entirety rather than by theme or series. To do this, I played with the notion of immensity: I wanted visitors entering the room to be unable to see its end,” the curator confides. Gelatin silver and palladium prints, in color and in black and white, are arranged along the walls, forming mysterious connections: so many nods to a secret narrative thread that one gets lost trying to uncover.

One floor up, Raymond Depardon’s “La France” takes the opposite approach to this avalanche of images. Here, the photographs, made with a large-format view camera, follow a route conceived as a reference to the photographer’s own approach. “He wanted to turn his gaze on a France in transformation that we never look at. From 2004 to 2010, he traveled the country in a van and chose to take only one shot per location,” says Matthieu Humery. The result is a body of 300 images, 50 of which are shown in “Remember Me”: the fruit of long-term work in which the immediacy of composition meets the slowness imposed by the chosen technique. Hung on the walls, but also on either side of the room and suspended from the ceiling, the photographs seem, through their arrangement, to invite us on a kind of journey to discover them better.

Big names and experiments

On the top floor of the Bourse de Commerce, the group show brings the exhibition to a close. It is organized into several themes: “By the Sea,” “Sérialité et typologie” (Seriality and Typology), “La fabrique de l’image” (The Making of the Image), “L’art de la composition” (The Art of Composition), “Le langage des mains” (The Language of Hands), “Face à face” (Face to Face) and “Le corps révélé” (The Body Revealed). Together they offer a selection of emblematic prints rooted in a rich photographic history. From one gallery to the next, big names rub shoulders with visual experiments; artists draw inspiration from one another, exchange nods and explore new ways of creating. Among them is an 1854 image by Roger Fenton, the oldest in the collection, which owes much to the paintings of Turner.

Further on, visitors come across Man Ray’s solarizations and Weegee’s distortions, Annie Leibovitz’s iconic portrait of John Lennon and Yoko Ono, and portraits by August Sander printed by his son. There is also a sculpture by Brancusi that inspired Man Ray’s famous Noire et Blanche (1926), a motif taken up by Edward Steichen with his model Anna May Wong in 1930, then reimagined by John Edmonds in Tête d’Homme in 2018. Richard Avedon, Cindy Sherman, Hiroshi Sugimoto, Dora Maar, Dorothea Lange… A true anthology, “Remember Me” showcases emblematic work and offers the public an ideal journey for the bicentenary.

“Remember Me” is on view at the Bourse de Commerce , in Paris, until January 18, 2027.
excerpt_original: At the Bourse de Commerce in Paris, the Pinault Collection puts photography center stage with “Remember Me,” a choral exhibition where iconic artists meet visual experiments. L’article Living Memory at the Bourse de Commerce est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

editorial_title_zh: Frieze Sculpture 2026：在伦敦公园中，雕塑变得混杂
editorial_excerpt_zh: 十一位艺术家将摄政公园转变为文化、记忆和材料之间混杂的实验室。从安吉尔·奥特罗到塔里尼·塞蒂，《Frieze Sculpture 2026：在伦敦公园中，雕塑变得混杂》一文来自exibart.com。

article_text:
Prima degli stand e dei corridoi, c’è il parco. Frieze Sculpture 2026 è la dimensione pubblica e all’aperto di Frieze London e Frieze Masters . Si tratta di un percorso di opere portate da gallerie internazionali, distribuite tra i prati e i viali di Regent’s Park, che accompagna la fiera offrendo a tutti un’esperienza gratuita dell’arte contemporanea. Undici artisti, undici modi di declinare la nozione di ibridazione, uniti dall’idea della scultura come linguaggio vivente, espanso e adattivo, che non si chiude in sé stesso ma dialoga con lo spazio, il paesaggio e chi lo attraversa. L’ingresso della quattordicesima edizione, per il quarto anno curata da Fatoş Üstek, è gratuito e la mostra resta aperta sette settimane, anche in coincidenza con Frieze London e Frieze Masters (14-18 ottobre). «Invitiamo i visitatori a uscire dai ritmi della vita quotidiana per entrare nel parco, dove le proposte artistiche aprono nuovi modi di pensare e di sentire», afferma la curatrice. Frieze Sculpture fa inoltre parte della London Sculpture Week (19-27 settembre), la celebrazione diffusa della scultura pubblica in città che riunisce cinque iniziative: Frieze Sculpture, Fourth Plinth, East Bank, Sculpture in the City e The Line.

Passeggiata nel parco: ecco le opere protagoniste di Regent’s Park

Dreams and Salt di Angel Otero , presentata dalla galleria Hauser & Wirth, è una scultura che raffigura una porta, quasi un portale che sembra scendere sotto la superficie del parco. Partendo dalla propria esperienza di attraversamento di geografie e culture, dall’infanzia a Porto Rico agli studi d’arte a Chicago, Otero trasforma la porta in un potente simbolo di migrazione e della distanza emotiva che si frappone tra una persona e la sua terra d’origine. Incassando una porta blu nel terreno e lasciandola socchiusa su un interno invisibile, l’artista crea una soglia che è al tempo stesso fisica ed emotiva.

Ramesh Mario Nithiyendran , presentato da Jhaveri Contemporary e Sullivan+Strumpf, lavora tra ceramica, fusione in bronzo, pittura e disegno e affronta l’ibridità da un’altra prospettiva. La sua Warrior Figure , alta due metri, ha due facce: da un lato un volto dipinto emerge dal bronzo texturizzato, richiamando gli oggetti votivi indù, buddisti e cristiani, dall’altro, un volto in bronzo lucidissimo riflette la luce circostante. Ne nasce un idolo guerriero immaginario, pensato per il presente, in cui storie frammentate e tradizioni diverse convivono in un’unica figura.

Prosegue la passeggiata nel parco. Metanoia di Ivana Bašić , selezionata da Albion Jeune rilegge gli Spomenik, i monumenti di guerra in cemento eretti nell’ex Jugoslavia per commemorare la Seconda guerra mondiale e tenere unita la comunità nazionale. Ne ricava una sorta di macchina che respira: un grappolo di forme simili a fiori di loto, in cemento, vetro e rame, i cui recipienti inspirano ed espirano attraverso collettori di scarico di auto da corsa. Segnata dai ricordi d’infanzia di violenza, l’opera si chiede che cosa resti quando gli ideali politici si spezzano e le identità si frammentano.

Davanti alla sua opera per Rajiv Menon Contemporary Tarini Sethi dice: «Si diventa parte di questa utopia»: chi guarda non è spettatore ma ne è parte. «Ciò che amo dell’acciaio inossidabile è la sua natura riflettente. Quando le persone si fermano davanti a una scultura in acciaio, il loro riflesso contribuisce all’opera». In The Sun Bathes Its Friends and Neighbours l’artista si appropria di materiali e simboli che in India sono ovunque, come l’acciaio inox, l’alluminio e l’arco, che rappresenta anche un ponte tra il mondo dei mortali e quello del divino. Attraversando la scultura si passa dal mondo di oggi a un mondo futuro che ciascuno può costruirsi da sé.

Il percorso di Frieze Sculpture 2026 si completa con le opere di Carolina Aguirre, presentata dalla galleria Ruttkowski;68, Matyáš Chochola , della Chemistry Gallery, Özlem Günyol e Mustafa Kunt , rappresentati da Dirimart, Catriona Robertson, presentata da The Muse Gallery, Conrad Shawcross, della galleria Victoria Miro, e Douglas White , presentato da Leila Heller Gallery.

Un ultimo riconoscimento riguarda il sostegno alle gallerie. La Mtec Bursary, istituita nel 2018 per aiutarle a coprire i costi di installazione e disinstallazione, è stata assegnata quest’anno a Dom Art Gallery per la nuova commissione di Elena Nemkova , Agony in the Garden (2026). Chi desidera approfondire le opere, anche a distanza, può affidarsi alla guida digitale gratuita di Bloomberg Connects, con contenuti esclusivi e un audio tour a cura di Üstek , scaricabile da Google Play o dall’App Store. Un modo per portare con sé, anche dopo la visita, l’invito a guardare il parco con occhi nuovi.

article_text:
To mark his eightieth birthday, the Czech photographer Jindřich Štreit shows a broad selection of silver gelatin prints, several of them never exhibited before, at the Centre tchèque de Paris, as part of the Photo Days festival.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Jindřich Štreit.

Jindřich Štreit was born in 1946 in Vsetín, in Moravia, to a schoolteacher father who kept a camera for pleasure. The boy wanted one of his own. His father agreed to pay for it on a single condition: that his son promise not to smoke for ten years. The boy, who had never touched a cigarette, promised. He took up his father’s trade, teaching children in the village schools of the country’s north before running the one at Jiříkov and keeping his village’s official chronicle.

In 1981, Jindřich Štreit photographed the general elections and the meetings of the local authorities, where the portrait of President Gustáv Husák turned up in the unlikeliest of places. The secret police shut down Setkání, the group show that put those pictures on a Prague wall in 1982, seized the prints and arrested him. Four months in Ruzyně prison followed, then a ten-month suspended sentence for defaming the republic and its head of state.

Stripped of his school and his right to exhibit, Jindřich Štreit wound up a dispatcher on a state farm. Nothing interrupted his census of faces. The Velvet Revolution cleared his name in 1989. The photographer then set his bags down in France, where he worked freelance in the early 1990s. “The village is a world,” as he puts it. In one of these pictures, a small girl in a cap spreads sheets of portraits across a table, her eyes wide.

Nearly 80 silver gelatin prints make up the Paris hang, among them a previously unseen series drawn from the original negatives. An accordionist plays in a yard cluttered with split firewood while a woman laughs, head thrown back. Further along, a couple hold each other against a wooden fence, eyes closed. Visitors may catch the familiar outline of their own grandparents, or a neighbor’s smile, behind these weathered faces and their tender gaze. If Jindřich Štreit has had only a camera for a tool, humanity has always served as his compass.

“Humanité” (Humanity) by Jindřich Štreit is on view at the Centre tchèque de Paris , 18 rue Bonaparte, Paris 6e, from November 5, 2026, to January 16, 2027. Free entry, Tuesday to Saturday, 1 to 7 p.m.

Curated by Emmanuelle de l’Écotais and Štěpánka Stein, with Štěpánka Bieleszová, and organized with Prague’s Teleport gallery, the show is part of Photo Days (November 2–30, 2026).
